issues.title: Egypt: Investigating severe broadband throttling after monthly data caps
issues.body:
**

# Egypt: Investigating severe broadband throttling after monthly data caps

Hello everyone,

I'm looking for technical insights into residential broadband throttling in Egypt.

**ISP:** Telecom Egypt (WE)

**Issue:** After the monthly data allowance is exhausted, some residential plans are reduced to approximately **256 Kbps**.

WE also advertises special access arrangements for certain educational and government websites. Examples include:

- https://digital.gov.eg
- https://mcit.gov.eg
- https://tra.gov.eg
- https://www.ekb.eg
- https://maharatech.gov.eg

The exact behavior of these exemptions after quota exhaustion may vary.

I would appreciate technical guidance on the following questions:

1. How can users distinguish an account-wide bandwidth limit from traffic-specific throttling?
2. What privacy-preserving tests could determine whether certain services retain higher speeds?
3. Are there legitimate VPN or network optimizations that improve usability on a 256 Kbps connection?
4. Are there existing open-source tools or research projects that investigate comparable ISP policies?

I understand that a VPN cannot necessarily remove a hard account-level speed cap.

My goal is to understand the technical restrictions and identify practical, measurable improvements.

For personal safety reasons, I prefer to remain anonymous and ask that no personally identifying information be requested publicly.

Thank you for any technical insights or references.

**

issues.title: Nakis: a TLS tunnel proxy built around connection reuse and write coalescing (efficiency first, circumvention effect unverified)
issues.body:
Hello all,

I would like to share a small project and ask for feedback from people who know this area better than I do. Nakis is a SOCKS5-in, TLS-tunnel-out proxy written in Go. Its main goal is transfer efficiency: get a ready tunnel to the application with as little waiting as possible, and keep per-write overhead low. Resistance to DPI was a secondary concern. I have not tested it against any real censor, so please read the DPI-related parts as hypotheses.

Repo: https://github.com/n-yarvex/nakis (MIT). The wire format and notes on the reference implementation are in doc/SPEC.md.

## Where the waiting goes

Most browser sessions are short, so the cost is dominated by setting up a tunnel: TCP, TLS, then whatever authentication the protocol adds. Nakis tries to take that off the critical path.

**Pre-connected pool.** The client keeps tunnels that have already finished the TLS handshake and authentication. A new session takes one from the pool and starts sending right away. This is always on, because turning it off could only make things slower.

**Reuse.** When a session ends, each side sends a zero-length frame (called NAP in the spec) for its own direction. Once both have been seen, no error occurred, and the tunnel has not used up its lifespan, it goes back to the pool and the next session reuses it without a new handshake. Each tunnel draws its own lifespan: a number of sessions (by default between 4 and 8) and a byte budget (log-uniform between 8 and 256 MiB), so there is no fixed "Nth session" or "Nth byte" boundary.

**Racing when the pool is empty.** The client dials several candidate addresses: the first two immediately, the rest staggered by 50 ms. The first to finish the handshake serves the session. The others are not thrown away; they go into the pool. The idea is mostly for lossy links and servers with several addresses, where one slow path should not stall everything.

## Write coalescing

Many proxies write each application read as its own frame. Nakis puts a queue (a "Box") in front of the tunnel and decides when to flush ("Gate"). One frame is one Write, which under TLS ends up in one record.

- If the queue is empty and the last data arrived at least 40 µs ago, the chunk is sent immediately. This is meant to keep interactive small writes from being delayed.
- Otherwise chunks queue up and are packed greedily into one frame, up to `send_pack`. A chunk is never split; what does not fit waits for the next frame.
- The queue is flushed when it reaches `send_pack`, or comes within `send_tail` bytes (default 512) of it.
- If it is not full, a 250 µs timer runs. If more data arrived in the meantime, it waits another tick, up to `send_quiet` x 4 ticks. With `send_quiet=4` that means at most about 4 ms of merging while data keeps arriving, and at most 250 µs once it stops.
- Large reads (32766 bytes or more) bypass the queue after flushing what is already queued, to keep ordering.
- The server has a second layer: small upstream frames are merged into writes of up to `merge_pack` (default 20 KiB) towards the target. When the queue reaches `max_queue`, the server stops reading the tunnel and TCP backpressure slows the client.

The trade-off is plain: under sustained small writes, latency can rise by up to `send_quiet` milliseconds in exchange for fewer, larger records.

## Shaping the first packets

The first few packets of a session (up to eight per direction) get a randomly drawn target size, per tunnel, per session, per direction. The target is reached by coalescing application data first. Padding (a frame with length 0xFFFF) is only used if the data has not filled the target after 2 ms, so this does not work like a conventional padding scheme. For the first packet only, that wait is an added latency of up to 2 ms. The plan also looks at the destination port: for ports that usually carry TLS (443 and similar), it covers more packets and draws larger ones more often, on the guess that a TLS handshake is nested insi

comments.issue_title: [Russia] recent mass ip bans
comments.body:
Adding a few data points from Tatarstan, Russia (home ISPs: Rostelecom / Tattelecom / Dom.ru), measured September–November 2026.

**Hetzner is fully unreachable, not throttled.** From an ER-Telecom line, TCP connect to Hetzner succeeds (both Helsinki 95.217.255.81 and the German corporate range 213.133.116.44), but the TLS handshake is killed — `openssl s_client` returns no certificate, and HTTPS downloads return 0 bytes at any request size, including 8 KB. Vultr, Linode and Cloudflare were reachable from the same line at the same time. Scaleway behaved like Hetzner.

**Geo databases can disagree with hoster jurisdiction.** netcup (AS214996) resolves as **US** in both ipinfo and iplocation, despite being a German company. Worth checking if the exit country matters for your use case — it is not visible from the hoster's own description.

**Two measurement pitfalls that produced wrong conclusions on my side:**

- Cloudflare's speedtest endpoint returns **HTTP 403** from proxy addresses. The 1-byte response looks exactly like a censorship freeze at ~16 MB. I initially misread this as TSPU throttling of the node. Leaseweb and RWTH mirrors behave correctly and showed full 16 MB transfers through the same tunnel at the same moment.
- `nc -z` on macOS reports "closed" for known-good hosts (1.1.1.1, Yandex), so it is unusable for reachability testing here. `curl --resolve` and `openssl s_client` give correct results.

**SNI/IP correlation.** A commercial service I observed keeps its Reality SNI donor domain **in the same /24** as its Russian entry node, while its foreign node has no such correlation. Possibly a deliberate response to SNI/IP mismatch checks.

Questions, if anyone has data:

1. What is the typical lifetime of a foreign VPS address under personal load (1–3 devices, no resale) — weeks or months? Is there a hoster-dependent difference in address lifetime specifically, as opposed to latency?
2. Does keeping the Reality SNI donor in the same subnet/ASN as the server measurably help right now?
3. For a Russia-based entry relay, which providers survive longest in practice?

Happy to run specific tests from this vantage point if that would be useful.

issues.title: Fix end address of 198.18.0.0/15 in IsInReservedRange
issues.body:
The RFC 2544 benchmarking range in `IsInReservedRange` ends at `192.19.255.255` instead of `198.19.255.255`. Since the end is below the start, the `first <= ip <= last` check never matches, so 198.18.0.0/15 is not treated as reserved even with `reservedrange = true`.

Checked by calling `i2p::util::net::IsInReservedRange` from a `libi2pd.a` built at tag 3.0.0:

```
                 before         after
198.18.0.1       not reserved   reserved
198.19.255.254   not reserved   reserved
192.19.0.1       not reserved   not reserved
10.1.2.3         reserved       reserved
8.8.8.8          not reserved   not reserved
```

The typo is also in 2.59.0.

issues.title: Outbounds: Avoid circular dependencies with the built-in DNS
issues.body:
重写 Lua 文档的时候被迫写了下面加粗的这段，觉得十分不科学，应该把它做成和 targetStrategy 一样防环，没有大的副作用。各出站的行为也比较统一。

> ::: warning 循环依赖
任意查询交给内置 DNS 模块处理时，若选中 DNS 服务器的 `address` 不含 `+local`，则到该服务器的连接会交给路由。若 `address` 是域名，路由脚本可能再次调用内置 DNS 解析它。新的查询可能按 DNS 和路由规则顺利完成，也可能经过多个 DNS 服务器和出站，重新依赖尚未完成的解析，形成死循环。

> 为避免这种潜在的循环依赖，DNS 模块会将自身发起的所有连接标记为 `skipDNSResolve = true`。核心原生的路由模块不检查是否真的成环，而是据此标记简单粗暴地跳过 DNS 解析，直接杜绝成环可能；请求随后继续匹配其余规则并交给出站。Lua 脚本需要自行处理该标记，建议同样跳过解析，也可以按需扩展处理方式。

> **Freedom 出站不会检查 `skipDNSResolve`。若脚本将这类连接交给它，且其 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，就会再次调用内置 DNS 解析该域名。路由脚本无法干预出站的解析，需另行规避，不再赘述；其他出站的 `targetStrategy` 会像路由一样检查该标记跳过解析以避免成环。**

> 其他出站也有另一种成环路径。若代理出站的服务器地址为域名，且 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，出站就会调用内置 DNS 解析该地址。例如，出站 A 依赖 DNS A 的解析结果，而 DNS A 的查询又被送回出站 A，就会形成死循环；也可能先送到出站 B，再因解析 B 的服务器地址而回到 DNS A，形成更长的依赖链。这些出站与 DNS 之间的循环与路由脚本无关，需另行规避，此处不再赘述。

issues.title: XTLS Vision: Fix panic and silent data loss on oversized buffers
issues.body:
### Problem

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` splits an oversized buffer once and writes the whole remainder into a single new buffer, discarding the `ErrBufferFull` that `Write` returns:

```go
buffer2 := buf.New()
buffer2.Write(buffer1.BytesFrom(index))
```

Buffers longer than `buf.Size` reach it, because `buf.NewExisted` only enforces a minimum capacity and the gRPC transport wraps hunks of arbitrary size with it (`grpc/encoding/hunkconn.go:97`, `multiconn.go:78`). The remainder is truncated to exactly `buf.Size`, so `XtlsPadding` computes `paddingLen = buf.Size - 21 - buf.Size = -21` and `Buffer.Extend` slices `b.v[8192:8171]`, which panics and takes down the process. With the default split point of `buf.Size/2` the threshold is 12288 bytes.

### Fix

Copy the remainder out in chunks of at most `buf.Size-21`, the largest content `XtlsPadding` can fit, until nothing is left. Buffers up to `buf.Size` keep their previous two-piece shape, so normal traffic is unaffected.

### Verification

On unmodified `main` (`f781c687`), a 12288-byte buffer panics with `slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]`. With this change, inputs of 8213 / 12288 / 20000 / 65535 bytes produce 2 / 3 / 3 / 9 buffers, every byte preserved and no piece above `buf.Size-21`. For inputs up to `buf.Size` the output shape is unchanged across the range of split points.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go run ./infra/vformat -mode check` and `go test ./...` are clean; the three geodata-dependent packages fail identically on unmodified `main` here because `geoip.dat` / `geosite.dat` are absent locally.

I reproduced this at the function level with the same `buf.NewExisted` constructor the gRPC transport uses, not end-to-end through a live gRPC inbound.

### On scope

Kept inside `ReshapeMultiBuffer`. Rejecting `n < 0` in `Buffer.Extend` would swap one panic for another without addressing the truncation, and stopping `buf.NewExisted` from returning oversized buffers looks intended. Happy to take whichever shape you prefer.

Fixes #7369. Same panic signature as #2651, #5961 and #6072.

issues.title: panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
issues.body:
## Summary

A relay node (Xray terminates several inbounds and forwards everything through ONE VLESS+Reality+`xtls-rprx-vision` outbound to another Xray) crashes the whole process several times per hour with a negative-length `Extend` in `proxy.XtlsPadding`. All inbounds are dropped on every crash (about 1 s with `RestartSec=1`).

No `testseed` anywhere in the config (so this is not #5961's "invalid testseed" case). No mux: 0 `v1.mux.cool` connections in the log over 24 h.

## Panic (identical every time, only goroutine ids differ)

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]

goroutine 640 [running]:
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.(*Buffer).Extend(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/buffer.go:153
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.XtlsPadding(0xc00021f740, 0x0, 0xc0002e1a28, 0x1?, {0x19a0058, 0xc000254730}, {0xc000269200?, 0xc000730000?, 0xc00033fb40?})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:519 +0x79e
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.(*VisionWriter).WriteMultiBuffer(0xc0002e19e0, {0xc00047ea98, 0x1, 0x1})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:390 +0x5dd
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.copyInternal(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:99 +0x15a
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.Copy(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:116
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound.(*Handler).Process.func4()
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound/outbound.go:360 +0xc79
```

(v25.12.8, go1.25.5, linux/amd64, kernel 6.8, 1 vCPU. `Process.func3` on 25.6.8 — same frames.)

## Analysis

The high bound `8171` is exactly `buf.Size - 21`. In `XtlsPadding`:

```go
if paddingLen > buf.Size-21-contentLen {
    paddingLen = buf.Size - 21 - contentLen
}
...
newbuffer.Extend(paddingLen)
```

`[8192:8171]` means `newbuffer.end == 8192` and `paddingLen == -21`, i.e. `contentLen == 8192`: a full 8192-byte block reached `XtlsPadding` unsplit. `Extend` has no check for negative `n`, so `b.v[b.end:end]` panics with low > high (the `end > len` check only guards the upper side).

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` is supposed to prevent this (it splits every block with `Len() >= buf.Size-21`), and `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` calls it right before the loop, so a full block should not get through. I could not find the path by reading the code (`XtlsPadding` and `ReshapeMultiBuffer` are byte-identical in v25.12.8 and v26.11.9). Possibilities I could not exclude: a buffer that is mutated/re-used between `ReshapeMultiBuffer` and `XtlsPadding` (pool double-release?), or a block larger than `buf.Size` entering through a non-standard reader.

Cheap hardening regardless of root cause: clamp `paddingLen` at 0 (`if paddingLen < 0 { paddingLen = 0 }`) and/or reject `n < 0` in `Buffer.Extend`. That would turn a process-wide crash into a (harmless) missing padding. Note that `newbuffer.Write(b.Bytes())` also silently truncates if `contentLen + 21 > 8192`, so the root cause is worth fixing too.

## Environment / what was tried

- Topology: several inbounds (Reality-TCP-Vision, Reality-TCP-Vision with self-steal dest, XHTTP+TLS, gRPC+TLS) → one VLESS+Reality+Vision outbound → Xray 25.6.8 server.
- Panics occur with users of ALL four inbounds (so not specific to one inbound transport).
- Versions tried as the relay: 25.6.8 (~1 panic / 5–10 min), 25.9.5 (2 in 1h20m), 25.12.8 (~6 / hour, 434 in 3 days, clustered: up to 5 within a minute). Not yet tried: 26.x on this node (26.10.31/26.11.9 server side breaks sing-box Reality clients in our tests, so we cannot deploy it for production users).
- Config has no `testseed`; `flow: xtls-rprx-vision` only.
- Related: #2651 (same signature, fixed in 2023), #5961 (same signature on 26.2.6/26.3.27, closed with "don't set testseed"), #6072.

## Expected

No process-wide panic on any input to the Vision writer.

issues.title: HTTP & SOCKS inbounds: Add `email` to access log
issues.body:
Fixes #7436.

HTTP and SOCKS inbounds store the authenticated login in `inbound.User.Email`, which `user` routing rules already match, but their access messages leave `Email` empty. This sets it on the HTTP, SOCKS TCP and SOCKS UDP access messages, as VLESS, VMess, Trojan, Shadowsocks and Hysteria already do. #5870 fixed the same symptom, an empty `Email` in Hysteria's access log, from a different cause.

`inbound.User` is assigned unconditionally at the top of both `Process` functions, so it is never nil at these sites. Without `accounts`, `Email` stays empty and the lines are unchanged.

Tested on `f781c68` with this commit, HTTP, SOCKS TCP, SOCKS UDP, and HTTP sent to the SOCKS port:

```text
from 127.0.0.1:39574 accepted //example.com:443 [http-in -> direct-out] email: alice
from tcp:127.0.0.1:44056 accepted tcp:example.com:443 [socks-in -> direct-out] email: bob
from udp:127.0.0.1:43730 accepted udp:1.1.1.1:53 [socks-in -> direct-out] email: bob
from 127.0.0.1:44086 accepted //example.com:443 [socks-in -> direct-out] email: bob
```

With `accounts` removed and SOCKS `"auth": "noauth"`, both TCP lines are unchanged.

issues.title: HTTP and SOCKS inbounds: access log omits the user's `email`
issues.body:
## Description

On v26.11.9, `accepted` access-log lines from HTTP and SOCKS inbounds with `accounts` have no ` email: <user>` suffix, although the user is authenticated and known to the core.

In the log below, the default outbound is `blackhole`, and only the rule `{ "user": ["alice", "bob"], "outboundTag": "direct-out" }` leads to `direct-out`. Both requests take `direct-out` and succeed, yet neither `accepted` line names the user (timestamps trimmed):

```text
from 127.0.0.1:47838 accepted //example.com:443 [http-in -> direct-out]
from tcp:127.0.0.1:33158 accepted tcp:example.com:443 [socks-in -> direct-out]
```

Other inbounds with users set `Email` in their access messages: VLESS ([inbound.go#L597](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/vless/inbound/inbound.go#L597)), VMess ([inbound.go#L261](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/vmess/inbound/inbound.go#L261)), Trojan ([server.go#L240](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/trojan/server.go#L240)), Shadowsocks ([server.go#L231](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/shadowsocks/server.go#L231)) and Hysteria ([server.go#L154](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/hysteria/server.go#L154)).

Both inbounds do store the login as the user's email: HTTP at [proxy/http/server.go#L127](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/http/server.go#L127), SOCKS at [proxy/socks/server.go#L136](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/socks/server.go#L136). Their access messages are built without it: HTTP at [#L148](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/http/server.go#L148), SOCKS TCP at [#L147](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/socks/server.go#L147) and SOCKS UDP at [#L268](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/v26.11.9/proxy/socks/server.go#L268).

So when several accounts share one HTTP or SOCKS inbound from the same client host, the access log can't tell which account made a request.

Expected: the two lines end with ` email: alice` and ` email: bob`, as access lines from the inbounds above do.

## Reproduction Method

1. Start Xray v26.11.9 with the server config below: `xray run -c config.json`.
2. Send one request through each inbound:

```sh
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -x http://alice:alice-pass@127.0.0.1:10809 https://example.com
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -x socks5h://bob:bob-pass@127.0.0.1:10808 https://example.com
```

issues.title: FakeDNS: avoid repeated allocation scans with a fixed-width cursor
issues.body:
FakeDNS currently chooses a starting address from the current millisecond on every cache miss. During a burst of queries for new domains, successive allocations repeatedly scan the same occupied addresses. This work happens under the holder mutex, so it also delays other queries using that holder, even when the pool has plenty of free addresses.

Keep an allocation cursor between queries instead. This removes the repeated scans in that workload and fixes address-width loss in the same allocation path.

## What changes

- Store a `netip.Addr` cursor per holder, initialize it once at a random address inside the configured pool, and continue from the previous allocation.
- Advance past occupied addresses and wrap at the pool boundary, including overflow at the end of the IPv4 or IPv6 address space.
- Preserve the existing allocation lock, LRU eviction and reverse-lookup behavior. Integer capacity validation requires a positive LRU size smaller than the pool, leaving a free address available before insertion.

The current `big.Int.Bytes()` conversion drops leading zero bytes. On unmodified upstream `f781c687`, a local reproduction returned a nil address for `0.1.0.0/16` and an IPv4 address for the IPv6 pool `::100:0/112`. Fixed-width addresses preserve the configured family and make these pools return valid, in-pool answers.

## Measured effect

A local microbenchmark allocates the same 4,096 distinct names in a fresh default IPv4 holder on each iteration. Three samples, five iterations per sample, on Windows amd64 with Go 1.27.3 and an Intel Core i5-11600K:

| Per 4,096-name burst | Upstream | This change |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Time | 861–956 ms | 1.70–3.68 ms |
| Allocations | 21.1–21.8 million | About 39,800 |

These measurements cover the allocator workload, not end-to-end proxy throughput. Occupied addresses still require probing; this does not make every allocation constant-time.

## Validation

- Existing FakeDNS and cache package tests passed.
- Additional local checks compared 493,568 operations with an independent LRU model, covering every starting address and valid cache capacity in twelve small IPv4/IPv6 pools. These included leading-zero addresses, address-space limits and IPv4-mapped IPv6 notation.
- 262,144 concurrent forward/reverse lookup pairs passed, with final uniqueness checks.
- A built Xray process answered repeated A and AAAA queries over loopback using an ordinary FakeDNS configuration.
- Focused regressions also ran on Windows 386; the FakeDNS tests compiled for Linux amd64 and macOS arm64. The Go race detector was not run.

Only `app/dns/fakedns/fake.go` changes. The cursor lasts for the holder's lifetime; it does not persist mappings across core restarts or change the existing consequences of LRU eviction for applications retaining old fake addresses.

issues.title: upgrade klauspost/compress to fix (CVE-2026-116591)
issues.body:
Updates github.com/klauspost/compress from v1.20.1 to v1.20.4 to address CVE-2026-116591 (GHSA-fpmh-frq8-7rj8).

Xray indirectly uses the Zstandard decoder through uTLS to decompress server certificate messages during TLS 1.3 handshakes. A crafted Zstandard frame can trigger an out-of-bounds panic in the affected decoder, potentially terminating the process when this certificate compression path is used.

Advisory: https://github.com/klauspost/compress/security/advisories/GHSA-fpmh-frq8-7rj8

### Validation

A standalone streaming-decoder reproducer was run against both versions using the same 27,567-byte input:

- v1.20.1: panics with `index out of range [33077] with length 32768` in a decoder worker goroutine, terminating the process.
- v1.20.4: returns `corrupt input: weights tableLog too big` with zero output and exits without a panic.

issues.title: uTLS: Pick `random` only from fingerprints that have X25519MLKEM768
issues.body:
Since v26.9.9, REALITY servers reject Client Hello that doesn't have X25519MLKEM768 before optional X25519 (https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/commit/8cdf7bf9c7f0), which is intended according to https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7259.

However, 7 of 12 `random` candidates don't have X25519MLKEM768: `hellofirefox_120`, `hellochrome_120`, `helloios_13`, `helloios_14`, `helloedge_106`, `hello360_11_0`, `helloqq_11_1`. `random` is chosen once at startup, so a REALITY client with `"fingerprint": "random"` can't connect at all until restart, with a chance of about 58% (`random` is also FAIL in the table of #7259).

This PR keeps only the candidates that have X25519MLKEM768: `hellofirefox_148`, `hellochrome_131`, `hellochrome_133`, `hellochrome_155`, `hellosafari_26_3`. The others are moved to `OtherFingerprints`, so their names still work. Nothing changes for explicitly named fingerprints.

Testing (local VLESS + Vision + REALITY server and client, `"fingerprint": "random"`, 12 starts each):

- before: 7 of 12 starts could connect
- after: 12 of 12 starts could connect

`go test ./transport/internet/tls/` and `TestVlessRealityFingerprints` pass.

issues.title: XDRIVE: when the client disappears mid-download, the server uploads the rest of the response and keeps the session for minutes
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

issues.title: Routing: Add `RegisterProcessFinder` for `process` on all platforms
issues.body:
The routing rule `process` calls `net.FindProcess` for each new connection. The lookup keeps no cache:

- On Windows, each call gets the full TCP or UDP table from the system.
- On Linux, each call reads the socket tables in `/proc/net`. Then it reads the links in `/proc/<pid>/fd` of each process.

With many sockets, each call is slow. A benchmark opened 100 or 1000 TCP connections on 127.0.0.1. Each connection has two sockets. Then the benchmark measured `net.FindProcess` for the client socket of the last connection. It ran with Xray-core v26.10.31 in two VMs with 2 virtual CPUs: Windows 10 22H2 and Ubuntu 26.04. On Linux, it ran as root.

| System | Sockets | Median | 99th percentile |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows | 200 | 186 µs | 285 µs |
| Windows | 2000 | 2.06 ms | 3.57 ms |
| Linux | 200 | 3.09 ms | 3.53 ms |
| Linux | 2000 | 8.87 ms | 9.61 ms |

An application that embeds Xray-core can use a faster method of its platform, for example netlink `sock_diag` on Linux. It can also keep a cache of the socket tables between connections. A hook gives the application this choice. The lookup of each platform stays as it is. On Android, an application can already register its own finder with `RegisterAndroidProcessFinder`.

This pull request adds such a hook for all platforms:

- `net.RegisterProcessFinder(f)` replaces the lookup of the platform with `f`. A nil finder restores the lookup of the platform.
- `net.FindProcess` calls the registered finder. Without a registered finder, it calls the lookup of the platform, as before.
- Xray-core can call the finder from many goroutines at the same time. Thus the finder must be safe for concurrent use.
- If an application registers both finders on Android, `net.FindProcess` calls only the finder of `RegisterProcessFinder`. `RegisterAndroidProcessFinder` stays as it is.
- The lookup of each platform has the new name `findProcess`. Its code has no other change.

Without a registered finder, the behavior does not change. With the hook, each call loads one atomic pointer. `TestRegisterProcessFinder` tests the hook.

issues.title: [Feature] XMC: Yggdrasil third-party login + texture signature verification / XMC 支持 Yggdrasil 第三方登录与材质签名验证
issues.body:
> Status: proposal / ready for discussion. Branch: `feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login` (based on `c4561418`), commits `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`.
> 状态：提案，欢迎讨论。分支：`feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login`（基于 `c4561418`），提交 `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`。

---

## 中文

### 背景与动机

当前 XMC 的登录认证是自造的：

- 客户端配置里手工填写 `username` / `uuid` / `texturesValue` / `texturesSignature`（需要自己去 Mojang 或皮肤站查 UUID、拉签名材质再复制进配置）；
- 服务端用预共享 `password`（同时作为 RSA 私钥的派生种子）加静态 `profiles` 白名单校验；
- Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，和 Minecraft 协议本身没有关系。

维护成本高，且无法复用 Minecraft 生态已有的标准在线模式认证（Yggdrasil / authlib-injector / Blessing Skin）。更重要的是，**如果后续要给 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端**（让真实 MC 客户端或服务端模组走标准 Yggdrasil 登录接入 XMC），预共享密码模型无法对接，因为模组侧只会实现标准的 `authenticate` / `join` / `hasJoined` 流程。

本次改动把 XMC 改成标准 Yggdrasil 登录客户端 + 标准 `hasJoined` 服务端校验，并补上材质签名验证，为后续 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端铺路，也为 XMC 客户端将来接入真实 MC 服务端打基础。

### 修改内容

涉及文件：

- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/yggdrasil.go`（新增：Yggdrasil HTTP 客户端、登录/刷新/join/hasJoined、验签）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/client.go`（Yggdrasil 登录、标准 hash、材质验签接入）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/server.go`（hasJoined 校验、随机密钥、断连语义）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/profile.go`（多 properties 读写、身份/材质比较）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/config.go`、`config.proto`、`config.pb.go`
- `infra/conf/transport_finalmask.go`（`yggdrasil` 配置解析、随机密钥生成、警告输出）
- 测试：`yggdrasil_test.go`、`profile_test.go`、`handshake_test.go`、`infra/conf/transport_finalmask_xmc_test.go`

#### 1. 配置

XMC `settings` 新增可选的 `yggdrasil` 段：

```json
{
  "type": "xmc",
  "settings": {
    "hostname": "mc.example.com",
    "yggdrasil": {
      "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil",
      "username": "user@example.com",
      "password": "<skin account password>",
      "player": "Steve"
    }
  }
}
```

- `api`：Yggdrasil API root（例如 Blessing Skin 的 `/api/yggdrasil`）；
- `username` / `password`：客户端登录凭据（邮箱或角色名，取决于 API 实现）；
- `player`：可选；账号有多个角色时必须指定；
- 服务端只需要 `api`，不需要账号密码。

Yggdrasil 模式下顶层 `password` 不再参与握手和密钥派生；旧配置（无 `yggdrasil` 段）行为完全不变。

#### 2. 客户端（client.go / yggdrasil.go）

- 通过 `authserver/authenticate` 登录，多角色时用 `authserver/refresh` 携带 `selectedProfile` 绑定 token；token/clientToken 进程内缓存，`/join` 遇到 403 自动重新登录重试一次。
- Login Start 使用皮肤站返回的真实角色名和 UUID。
- 加密协商完成后按原版算法计算 login hash：

  `sha1(serverId + sharedSecret + serverPublicKey)`，并按 Java `BigInteger#toString(16)` 的二进制补码规则渲染（包含负号和去前导零）。

- **使用 Encryption Request 中实际收到的公钥计算哈希，不再固定配置公钥**；Yggdrasil 模式客户端不需要也不应该去“确认公钥”。
- 用 `accessToken` 真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/join`。
- 解析 Login Success 的多个 properties，并用 API root 中的 `signaturePublickey` 校验 `textures` 属性签名：
  - SHA1withRSA（与 Blessing Skin 的 `openssl_sign` 默认算法、Minecraft 客户端的签名校验一致）；
  - 支持 PEM / 裸 base64 公钥；
  - 公钥按账号缓存，验签失败时自动重新拉取一次（覆盖皮肤站轮换密钥）；
  - `textures` 缺失、无签名、签名不匹配都会拒绝登录；
  - 校验发生在发送 Login Acknowledged 之前，失败不会进入 play 阶段。
- Yggdrasil 模式不再往 Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，保持和原版客户端一致的报文形状。

#### 3. 服务端（server.go）

- Yggdrasil 模式下每个进程随机生成 1024-bit RSA 密钥对（与原版服务端行为一致），**不再从 password 派生**；
- 解密共享密钥后，用自己实际持有的公钥计算同一个 login hash，真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/hasJoined`；
- 因为客户端 `/join` 与服务端 `/hasJoined` 存在天然竞态，服务端以 200ms 间隔轮询，最长 10s；
- 校验返回的角色 UUID / 名称必须与 Login Start 一致；
- Login Success 直接使用 `hasJoined` 返回的已签名 properties（含 `textures`、`uploadableTextures`）；
- 失败时按原版语义断连：未加入 → `multiplayer.disconnect.unverified_username`，API 异常 → `multiplayer.disconnect.authservers_down`；
- 未配置 `yggdrasil` 时保留原预共享密码 + `profiles` 白名单逻辑。

#### 4. 安全模型与警告

Yggdrasil 模式的安全绑定发生在 Yggdrasil 查询里：中间人两侧分别握手时，客户端提交的 hash 和服务端查询的 hash 必然不同，`hasJoined` 返回空，连接失败；即使不固定服务端公钥也无法完成中间人。

由于这时不再使用预共享密码、也不做密码派生，控制台会在 config 加载时输出一次警告（`errors.LogWarning`）：

```text
XMC: Yggdrasil mode is enabled. The RSA key pair is generated randomly and "password"
is no longer used to derive it or to authenticate the transport; players are verified
through https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil (client /join, server /hasJoined).
Both ends must be able to reach the Yggdrasil API. The configured "password" is ignored.
```

### 兼容性

- 不配置 `yggdrasil`：完全保持旧行为（密码派生密钥 + verify to

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Yggdrasil third-party login and texture verification
issues.body:
Refs #7394 (proposal). **Draft for review, not ready to merge.**

## What this adds

- **Yggdrasil third-party login.** The XMC client can authenticate against a third-party Yggdrasil API (Blessing Skin / authlib-injector compatible), join the Minecraft session with the standard vanilla login hash and reuse the API's signed textures. The XMC server verifies players through `sessionserver/session/minecraft/hasJoined` instead of a hand-copied profile list.
- **Texture verification and key handling.** In Yggdrasil mode the RSA key pair is no longer derived from the password: each side generates its own key pair, the client accepts the key sent in Encryption Request and binds it through the session hash, and the server verifies with its own actual public key through `/hasJoined`. The client verifies the signed `textures` property with the API's `signaturePublickey` (SHA1withRSA), refreshing the key once if a rotation is detected.
- **Generated config.** `config.pb.go` is regenerated with `infra/vprotogen` for the new `Yggdrasil` message and `Config.yggdrasil = 13`.

Files: `yggdrasil.go` (new), `client.go`, `server.go`, `profile.go`, `config.go`, `config.proto` (`Config.yggdrasil = 13`), `infra/conf/transport_finalmask.go`, plus tests.

## Rebased onto #7402

The branch now sits on current `main` (`f781c687`, #7402 "Switch to native frame padding" merged). Conflicts resolved as follows:

- `Padding` in `config.proto`/`config.pb.go` keeps `main`'s `length_min`/`length_max`/`direction`/`delay_min`/`delay_max`; `config.pb.go` regenerated with `infra/vprotogen` instead of hand-merged.
- The legacy password checks added by #7402 (`empty password`, `MaxLegacyPasswordLength`) moved into the legacy branch of `XMC.Build`, so Yggdrasil mode does not require a password (it is ignored there) while the legacy path keeps both checks.
- `newClientConn`/`wrapConnServer` call sites updated for the new `paddings` + `auth` parameters (including `config_test.go`).

## Compatibility

- No `yggdrasil` section: the legacy pre-shared password + `profiles` path is unchanged.
- With `yggdrasil`: `password` is ignored (a console warning is printed) and `profiles` is not required.
- `Config.yggdrasil = 13` keeps existing configs that already use `paddings = 12` working unchanged.

## What this waits on

- #7394 is still a proposal, so this PR is for review only.
- The server-side target — a Fabric mod on a real Minecraft 26.1 server that only bridges `xmc:data` — is still pending. #7402 switched startup padding to native Minecraft frames, so the mod no longer has to tear down vanilla's splitter.
- End-to-end verification against a real `26.1` (protocol `775`) server is still pending: the public XMC test domain and its `authlib-skin` are gone, so the harness needs a local Yggdrasil API. It is planned together with #7423 (draft: padding guards + zlib write framing), where that harness already exists.
- CI: first-time contributor PR, workflows need maintainer approval.

## Tests

Locally, on top of `f781c687`:

```text
go build ./...                                         # pass
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc ./infra/conf   # pass
go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./      # pass
go run ./infra/vprotogen/main.go -mode check -pwd ./    # pass
```

issues.title: XMC: prevent deadlock during bidirectional startup padding
issues.body:
XMC startup padding can deadlock after #7402 when both directions exceed the connection buffers. Both endpoints write their entire local schedule before starting the packet reader, so neither drains the peer's padding and both writes eventually time out.

Drain incoming `xmc:pad` packets while sending startup padding. Retain the first non-padding packet and then hand reading back to the packet stream, buffering at most one packet. The padding wire format and configured pauses are preserved. A startup write failure closes the connection to release the pending reader.

For example, this valid schedule can stall both endpoints:

```json
"paddings": [
  {"direction": "c2s", "length": "8388608"},
  {"direction": "s2c", "length": "8388608"}
]
```

The regression test exercises the full encrypted handshake over `net.Pipe` with 64 KiB turns and TCP with 8 MiB turns and constrained socket buffers, followed by proxy data in both directions. The pipe handshake failed on both endpoints before the fix. Reader tests cover preserving following packets, read errors, empty reads, and connection closure.

Checked the 57 currently open PRs: only #7423 and #7416 modify XMC. #7423 handles schedule bounds/cancellation and #7416 handles authentication; neither adds concurrent padding reads.

Validation passed:

```text
go test -p=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/... ./infra/conf -count=1
go test -p=1 -race ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc -count=1
go run -p=1 ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
```

issues.title: XMC: bound padding schedules, fix delay placement, stop compressing frames
issues.body:
Follow-up to #7402, rebased onto `main` now that #7402 has merged: this is no longer a stacked draft, the diff is four commits, and it also settles the delay question and the compression side effect that #7402 left behind.

1. **Bound padding schedules and cancel their pauses on Close** (unchanged from the draft). Padding pauses are timers that watch a per-connection `done` channel; a configured schedule is rejected above 256 turns, 64 MiB of turns, or the handshake deadline minus ten seconds of pauses; an explicit empty `paddings` array (or `"noPadding": true`) disables padding, and an absent field keeps the preset.

2. **Pause before a padding turn and never after the last one**. A configured `delay` used to be applied *after* its turn, so the last turn of a schedule paused even though nothing followed it: with `delay: "300"` on the final turn the first proxied packet went out 300 ms later, while both ends otherwise waited for nothing. The pause now leads into the turn it is configured on - a captured gap is written on the turn that follows it - and the last turn is not followed by a pause. Which value each end waits is unchanged and now stated in the proto comment: the side that sends the turn samples `[delay_min, delay_max]`, the peer spends exactly `delay_min` (it waits the minimum, not "at least" it), so a range jitters only the sending side and `delay_min == delay_max` reproduces a captured gap.

3. **State what a configured padding list replaces**. Two decisions only lived in the pull request: a configured list is the complete schedule, so the preset's Play-state join tail runs only with the preset; and a peer cannot be checked for arriving early, because the turns are ordinary Minecraft packets that the receiver leaves in the stream for the next reader to drop, with the pause bound covering a stalled peer. Both are now next to the code and pinned by a test.

4. **Never compress the frames XMC writes**. After `Set Compression` the writer deflated everything at or above the threshold, which is exactly the padding (zeros, ~300:1) and the proxied bytes (already compressed or encrypted): the padded shape disappeared and the CPU work bought nothing. The writer now always sends the uncompressed variant, which vanilla accepts at any size (`Data Length = 0` is not subject to the threshold check), and the reader still inflates what a real server sends.

## Tests

```text
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc ./infra/conf
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/...
go test -count=1 -race ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
go build ./...
go run ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
go run ./infra/vprotogen -pwd . -mode check
```

New coverage: pause placement for both roles and the absence of a trailing pause; which end samples the range and which spends the minimum; a configured list replacing the whole preset on both ends; the writer never compressing (zero-filled and random bodies, 1 B to 64 KiB) while the reader still accepts deflated bodies, chunked writes and multiple frames per write.

## End-to-end, real server, compression on

Local Fabric 26.1 server (protocol 775) with the server-side mod, `online-mode=true` through a local Yggdrasil API and authlib-injector, `network-compression-threshold=256` (the default), and a byte-counting relay in front of the server. The client side is this branch with the Yggdrasil draft #7416 merged locally for the real login.

| Measurement (threshold 256) | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client-to-server bytes for two 64 KiB padding turns | 889 B | 131,519 B |
| Upload 32 MiB through XMC | 19.2-20.9 MB/s | 46.9-52.1 MB/s |
| Download 32 MiB through XMC | - | 19.4-22.2 MB/s, sha256 OK |

The built-in preset and a configured schedule both log in and reach the tunnel, and the server accepts the uncompressed bodies above the threshold (padding frames of 32 KiB, tunnel frames of 24 KiB). A configured `delay` of 600 ms on two turns adds 1.2 s to the login as expected, s

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Switch to native frame padding (breaking); `delay` supports range (receiver waits at least minimal ms)
issues.body:
Follow-up to #6769 (merged in `5d17b872`): completes the remaining `delay` requirement and, per [this reply](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7402#issuecomment-6890345279), switches padding to the more realistic wire format even though that is a breaking change.

## Delay

- `delay` is now a **string**: `"100"` or `"50-150"` (milliseconds). A number written against #6769 no longer parses, so this is a configuration-level breaking change as well.
- The sender waits a uniformly sampled value in `[min, max]` after its turn.
- The receiver waits at least `min` after each turn, including the last one, before the proxy stream starts.
- `config.proto`: `delay` becomes `delay_min` / `delay_max`; negative, reversed and duration-overflowing ranges are rejected at config load.
- `infra/conf`: parses the string delay; tests cover fixed values, ranges and invalid forms.

## Native frame padding (`ea2c7edc`, breaking)

The opaque format wrote a length field that includes its own varint. A vanilla server therefore split the stream one header short and had to take the protocol pipeline over — something a Fabric server mod cannot do without affecting ordinary players.

- One padding chunk becomes one or more configuration-state custom payload frames on `xmc:pad`; the length field now has the vanilla meaning (bytes after the field).
- Chunks above the 32767-byte serverbound payload limit are split; captured 2-byte turns send the smallest possible frame.
- Nothing reads padding any more: it is ordinary traffic that the next reader drops as an unknown packet. Both ends only send and apply the configured pauses.
- The first turn still counts the two Login Acknowledged bytes as its prefix; they are not repeated.
- `maxPacketDataLength` is raised from 32 KiB to 1 MiB (vanilla's clientbound custom payload limit), which a real configuration state can reach with registry data.

**Breaking:** both ends must run this version. No proto field was added for padding; the `paddings` length/direction semantics are unchanged, and `delay` moved from a number to a millisecond string.

Example:

```json
"paddings": [
  {"length": "44", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "0"},
  {"length": "64-128", "direction": "s2c", "delay": "100"},
  {"length": "25", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "50-150"},
  {"length": "32768-49152", "direction": "s2c"}
]
```

Both endpoints should still use the same array and the same `delay` ranges, because that is what reproduces the captured shape. Nothing is compared against the peer's schedule any more, though: the receiver does not consume padding, so a length, direction or turn-count difference can no longer fail or stall the handshake, it only changes what each side sends.

## Scope

Per the cleanup in #6769, this PR does **not** restore the XMC `README.md` / `*_test.go` files deleted in that squash commit. The only new test file is `padding_frames_test.go`, which covers the frame plan/reachability and the source of the padding stream, because the wire format changed here.

## Tests

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
go build -o /tmp/xray-core-build ./main
go run ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
go run ./infra/vprotogen -pwd . -mode check
```

## Validation fix

A legacy password longer than 113 bytes is now rejected when the configuration is built (`035c45de`), instead of being accepted and then failing every handshake: the verify token plus the password must fit one RSA-1024 PKCS#1 v1.5 block (128-11 bytes), so `rsa.EncryptPKCS1v15` was failing on the client and the server could not decrypt it either.

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
```

issues.title: Routing: add server-only VMess UUID routes and online user cache
issues.body:
Allow ordinary VMess clients to select declared server-side routes by changing UUID bytes 7 and 8, with only the server upgraded and no account flag required. `userRoute` is the shared routing matcher; `vlessRoute` keeps its existing behavior.

README.md is unchanged in the PR diff.

## Behavior and compatibility

- Generate aliases only for explicit `routing.rules[].userRoute` values applicable to the inbound and user, including existing exact/regexp user matching. Destination-dependent conditions remain routing conditions; Lua-only routing declares no aliases.
- Preserve exact configured UUIDs and the original account's email, policy, statistics and API identity. The experimental account flag and wire extension have been removed completely. Account JSON/protobuf definitions and client encoding match the pre-feature source; no account option or wire field is added.
- Admit connections after normal authenticated header checks. Registration IDs, route generations and pending-change checks reject stale candidates across account/rule changes, including removal and re-addition of the same account object. Closed validators cannot rebuild catalogs.
- Retain identity history during an inbound's lifetime so a removed exact credential cannot become another user's generated alias. Different original route bytes mark the 14-byte identity ambiguous and disable its aliases. Exact credentials remain usable. History is not persisted: independently revocable users and credential rotations must use distinct non-route UUID bytes.
- Align Unicode email removal with the inbound's lowercase index. Retain AuthID replay entries for the full inclusive timestamp-validity interval using 241-second buckets; accepted clock skew and wire encoding remain unchanged. This retains more replay records under sustained traffic.

## Cache and resource bounds

Only authenticated online/recent accounts populate the prepared cache; there are no IP/source-address hints. Idempotent connection leases expire two minutes after the final close. Route changes preserve live leases and idle deadlines without refreshing recency. Search and eviction share one recency list, immutable provider declarations are copied before filtering, and rejected cache growth does not evict unrelated entries.

Per inbound: 64 MiB prepared-key payload, a 128 MiB raw-alias-key limit, and two concurrent alias scans. Oversized live catalogs preserve exact credentials while rejecting aliases. Metadata, replay records and temporary old/new catalog overlap are additional memory. Occupied scan slots can reject further alias handshakes, including hot-cache users; exact credentials bypass those slots.

The amd64 AES-NI/SSE4.1 search accelerator retains all ten AES rounds in a 68-byte schedule and rechecks candidates with the standard-library decoder. Unsupported CPUs, `purego`, and Go FIPS mode select the standard-library fallback. This is not a cryptographic certification or a claim of VLESS-equivalent lookup cost.

## Validation

- VMess, router/command, routing features and configuration tests passed, along with the complete VMess `purego` tests and repository formatting.
- After removing the experimental account flag, all 160 published-binary compatibility cases passed again using clients 1.8.24, 25.12.8 and 26.11.9: 120 ordinary VMess/VLESS cases in both directions, 33 UUID-only/negative/legacy-route cases, and seven byte-identical old-config compilation cases. Coverage includes TCP/UDP, AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305, Mux, and route values 0/300/65535.
- Known-answer AES plus 4,096 differential decryptions; malformed headers and replay; identity collisions/revocation; concurrent account/rule changes; and 4,000-operation cache lifecycle checks passed. Selected regressions also passed 30 repetitions at each of 1/2/4 CPUs with shuffled order, Go pointer checking, and runtime CPU-feature fallback.
- Windows executable and Linux amd64/arm64 VMess cross-builds passed. The full network scenario package passed

issues.title: Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: TLS : tls spoofing
issues.body:
fix #5964

### RawPacket aka TLS Spoofing

So first lets talk about the idea,

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

Here we append a TCP option with kind=19 and length=18 to the TCP header. The kind 19 is the MD5 signature option (RFC 2385), if the receiver doesn't use TCP MD5 (which is basically everything except some BGP routers), it sees an unknown option

issues.title: Move Browser Dialer to `sockopt.dialerProxy` `browser://` URL usage, with UUID path validation, startup-time conflict checks, instance-lifecycle listen/serve control, XHTTP mode constraints, and static initialization simplification
issues.body:
This PR moves Browser Dialer usage to `sockopt.dialerProxy` with `browser://host:port/uuid` URLs and removes the earlier parse-time listener startup side effects.

### What changed

- `dialerProxy` now uses `browser://host:port/uuid`
- Browser Dialer URLs are collected and validated during config build
- URL validation includes host:port parsing, UUID path validation, and same-port/different-IP conflict checks
- Browser Dialer remains restricted to WebSocket and XHTTP, with XHTTP limited to `auto` / `packet-up`, and REALITY rejected
- Listener startup is now controlled by the Xray instance lifecycle:
  - start in `core.Instance.Start()`
  - stop in `core.Instance.Close()`
- Startup failure cleanup now also tears down Browser Dialer listeners

### Scope

The change keeps the simplified non-dynamic model, but ties listener lifetime to the actual Xray instance instead of starting listeners while only parsing/building config.
