issues.title: gRPC transport: Do not read hunks larger than buf.Size into one buffer
issues.body:
Fixes https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7369

`HunkReaderWriter.ReadMultiBuffer` (and the multiMode reader) wraps a received hunk in one `Buffer` whenever `cap >= buf.Size`, so a hunk larger than 8192 bytes becomes one oversized buffer. Xray clients never send such hunks, but sing-box writes up to 32 KiB per hunk (its `buf.BufferSize`), and #7369 mentions sing-box clients.

When that buffer reaches a VLESS outbound with `xtls-rprx-vision`, `ReshapeMultiBuffer` copies the tail into a new 8 KiB buffer (`Write` silently drops the rest) and `XtlsPadding` gets `contentLen == 8192`, which gives `paddingLen == -21` and the panic in the issue:

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.(*Buffer).Extend(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.XtlsPadding(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.(*VisionWriter).WriteMultiBuffer(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.copyInternal(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.Copy(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound.(*Handler).Process.func4()
```

This PR keeps the zero-copy path only for hunks of at most `buf.Size` bytes; larger ones are read into standard buffers.

Reproduced on loopback with a relay like the one in #7369: VLESS gRPC inbound -> VLESS + TLS + Vision outbound -> VLESS Vision server -> echo server. The client writes hunks the way sing-box does and uploads 256 KiB:

| hunk size | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 4096, 8192 | ok | ok |
| 16384, 32768 | relay panics as above | ok, all bytes echoed |
| 32768, multiMode | relay panics as above | ok, all bytes echoed |

The new tests in `transport/internet/grpc/encoding` fail on main with `got a buffer of 8193 bytes, larger than buf.Size`.

issues.title: XDRIVE: Cancel pending storage operations on interrupt
issues.body:
## Problem

`common.Interrupt` falls back to `Close()` for an XDRIVE connection. `Close()` drains the writer before canceling the connection context. If storage is holding an upload, interruption waits for the very operation it needs to cancel. The asynchronous slot announcement also uses a background context, so it can remain pending after connection shutdown.

svlavr reported both behaviors while testing direct VLESS multiplexing. A mock backend reproduced them with a held upload and a held announcement. [Original report in #7415](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7415#issuecomment-6886431076)

## Design

`Interrupt()` cancels the session before entering the existing `Close()` path. Cancellation runs before the `sync.Once` guard, so it can wake a graceful close that is already waiting. Both slot and WAL writers stop admitting work after cancellation and wait for in-flight writes to finish unwinding before storage is released. A canceled drain skips the EOF marker.

The slot announcement now uses the session context and is part of the writer’s existing wait group. The context makes an interrupted publication cancelable. Joining it also lets a short graceful transfer finish publishing its session before `Close()` sends EOF and releases storage. This keeps the inline first-segment optimization and the existing wire format.

`Close()` still means graceful drain. Transport owners use `common.Interrupt` on the underlying connection when they need to abort. The direct Mux proposal already unwraps stats connections on its explicit interrupt path. [#7364](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7364)

## Validation

- Added regressions for interrupting an already-running `Close()` with a blocked slot or WAL upload, canceling a pending announcement, and allowing the announcement to finish during graceful close. All four cases detect the original behavior on upstream `main`.
- Passed the full XDRIVE suite on Windows with and without `-race`, plus 50 race-enabled repetitions of the shutdown regressions.
- Trial-merged this branch with #7415 and ran both sets of regressions together 10 times under `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

issues.title: DNS: Add `udp+local://` support
issues.body: Close #7321

issues.title: XDRIVE: Prevent ring-slot reuse before the previous upload completes
issues.body:
## Problem

The peer can acknowledge segment 0 from the inline session announcement while its upload to the ring is still in flight. With a ring of depth 2, that acknowledgement can admit the upload for segment 2 to the same slot. If the original upload finishes last, it overwrites segment 2 and leaves a gap in the stream.

This ordering reproduces the intermittent `TestSlotFirstAnnouncement` failure seen in two Ubuntu jobs. [November 13 job](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/actions/runs/43400976127/job/131803491599) and [November 14 job](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/actions/runs/43647865009/job/132609573715).

## Fix

- Require a successful previous write to the same slot and an acknowledgement from the existing cumulative watermark before reusing it.
- Keep checking the watermark while the local upload is pending. The reader-stall timeout applies while the acknowledgement is missing, so an acknowledged upload can finish retrying during `Close`.
- Propagate a terminal write error to queued reuse of the slot and retain the best-effort error frame for peers still waiting for that sequence.

The change uses the existing announcement, frame format, and acknowledgement protocol.

## Validation

- Extended `TestSlotFirstAnnouncement` to hold the first upload after the inline acknowledgement. The slow-write case verifies the complete byte stream through EOF. The failure case verifies that `Close` promptly returns the original write error and that the slot contains the error frame.
- Verified that the regression test detects premature reuse on upstream `main`. Both cases passed 100 times with the race detector on this branch.
- Passed the full `transport/internet/xdrive` suite on Windows with and without `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

issues.title: Routing: Fix Linux `process` for IPv4-mapped sockets
issues.body:
On Linux, a `process` rule misses IPv4 connections made from IPv6 (dual-stack) sockets, which Java and .NET open by default. Such a socket is listed in `/proc/net/tcp6` or `udp6` with an IPv4-mapped address, but for an IPv4 source the lookup reads only `/proc/net/tcp` and compares the IPv4 form. It is #6533 on Linux.

Fix: for an IPv4 source, also look for its IPv4-mapped address in the IPv6 file.

Test: `TestFindProcessIPv4Mapped` fails on main for TCP and UDP. With a real Java program through a SOCKS inbound, `"process": ["java"]` is skipped on main and matches with the fix.

issues.title: XHTTP/3 client: Close the UDP socket when the QUIC dial fails
issues.body:
When an XHTTP/3 dial fails, e.g. where QUIC is blocked, the `quic.Transport` made for it and its UDP socket are never closed. Each failed dial leaves one socket and two goroutines, so a client that keeps retrying runs out of file descriptors.

Fix: close both when `DialEarly` fails, as the MASQUE and XDRIVE dialers do. The socket goes first: `tr.Close()` waits for its read to return, which over `dialerProxy` would block the dial.

Test: `Test_DialQUICFailureClosesSocket` fails on main. 100 dials to a peer that never answers leave 100 sockets and 200 goroutines on main, none with the fix.

issues.title: Observatory: return independent snapshots under the status lock
issues.body:
`Observer.GetObservation` returns the internal status slice and its protobuf objects while background probes update and prune them. Callers can therefore observe changes after the method returns, race with updates during serialization, or accidentally mutate observer state.

Clone the observation under the existing status mutex. The returned message owns its slice, status objects, and nested messages; serialization happens after the lock is released. Probe scheduling, balancing behavior, and the protobuf API are unchanged.

Tests cover preservation of fields, snapshot stability after updates/additions/pruning, caller mutation of the slice and nested HealthPing message, empty results, and concurrent updates/pruning/readers/serialization. The isolation regression fails on unmodified main.

Validation:
- Windows: Observatory package tests, 100 repetitions of the new snapshot tests, balancer regression tests, and `go vet ./app/observatory/...` passed.
- Linux: `go test -race ./app/observatory/... -count=10` and balancer regression tests with `-race` passed in a separate validation branch containing the same source commit.
- Linux: `go vet ./app/observatory/...` and the repository-wide `vformat` check passed. The local Windows format check reported CRLF checkout differences; the clean Linux checkout passed.
- Full router tests were attempted locally but require the absent `resources/geosite.dat`; the targeted balancer tests passed.

Validation run: https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/actions/runs/43646303751

Refs #5117. This fixes snapshot safety in the existing Observatory API; it does not implement the remaining outbound-management features.

issues.title: UDP: avoid info-level read failure after local session termination
issues.body:
When the UDP idle timer or owner closes a session while `handleInput` is reading, termination cancels the context and interrupts the pipe. The read can return `io.ErrClosedPipe` after the loop's context check, producing an info-level `failed to handle UDP input` message for a local close.

Downgrade that error to debug only when this connection's local termination flag is set. Make the existing flag atomic because termination, input handling, and dispatcher reuse inspect it across goroutines. Unrelated read errors, closed-pipe errors without local termination, and parent cancellation alone retain the existing logging behavior. EOF handling and cleanup order are unchanged.

Tests exercise the real pipe interruption path, idle timeout, concurrent/repeated close, wrapped errors, unrelated errors during shutdown, parent cancellation, EOF, and the close callback count. The regression test fails on unmodified main with the original info-level message.

Validation on Windows/amd64:
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -count=1` passed.
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -run TestHandleInputTermination -count=100` passed.
- `go vet ./transport/internet/udp` and `git diff --check` passed.
- Local race-detector execution was unavailable: the environment has no CGO C compiler. Linux runtime tests were not run locally.

Refs #4621. This addresses local UDP termination only; it does not suppress remote resets or change general connection-error handling.

issues.title: XDRIVE: retry WAL segments that are visible before upload completes
HTTPUpgrade client: Close the connection when the upgrade fails
issues.body:
When the upgrade request could not be sent, or the server did not answer with a valid "101 Switching Protocols", the dial returned the error and left the TCP connection open until the garbage collector closed it.

With "fingerprint": "unsafe", a failed TLS handshake is one of these cases. Go's TLS does the handshake at the first write, and here the first write is the upgrade request.

issues.title: Keep the started gRPC server in the API goroutine
issues.body:
Stopping an API-enabled Xray instance immediately after `Start` can panic in `grpc.Server.Serve`. The serving goroutine reads `c.server` after `Close` has stopped the server and cleared the field. Both direct `api.listen` and tagged API listeners use this goroutine.

Capture the server created by that `Start` call and use it for service registration and serving. Treat `grpc.ErrServerStopped` as an expected shutdown result when `Close` wins the startup race. Listener cleanup follows gRPC's existing `Stop` and `Serve` behavior.

The regression uses real `core.New`, `Start`, and `Close` calls for both API configurations. It runs immediate start/stop cycles on one logical processor and yields to the API goroutine after shutdown. Each mode separately reproduces the nil receiver panic on the previous implementation.

Both regression cases pass on Windows and on Linux with `-race`. `go vet ./app/commander` passes on both platforms. The existing `TestCommanderListenConfigurationItem` and `TestCommanderRemoveHandler` integration tests also pass on Windows, exercising service registration and RPC calls for both listener modes.

AI-assisted implementation and tests.

issues.title: Wait for log writers to close on shutdown
issues.body:
On Windows, an application that shuts down Xray and immediately renames its log file can get a sharing violation. `Close` signals the log worker, which releases the file later when it exits.

Wait for the worker to release the writer before returning from `Close`. Ignore messages received after shutdown and check for shutdown again when acquiring the worker permit. In `app/log`, detach both handlers before waiting so a worker can finish formatting a message that itself records a log. Keep `Start` and `Close` serialized.

The regressions hold a real file writer open during message formatting, rename the file as soon as `Close` returns, and check that a late message cannot create another writer. Both regressions fail on the previous implementation. The Windows run reproduces the sharing violation.

`Close` can now wait for in-flight formatting and writes to finish. The message queue remains best effort.

Windows and Linux each passed all 14 tests in `./common/log`, `./app/log`, and `./app/log/command`. The Linux run used `-race`. `go vet` passed for all three packages on both platforms, and the Windows main build passed.

AI-assisted implementation and tests.

issues.title: Fix noise after udphop
issues.body:
Fix noise emission when `noise` and `udphop` are used together.

Previously, noise state was keyed by the destination passed to `WriteTo`. udphop could replace that destination internally or switch the source socket without invalidating the noise state. Continuous outgoing traffic also refreshed the noise reset timeout, allowing repeated hops without another noise sequence.

**Implementation**

- Add shared `UDPPath` state through the existing finalmask dialer, containing the actual destination, a generation counter, and a mutex.
- Increment the generation after a successful hop changes the local endpoint, destination IP, or destination port.
- Have the noise wrapper clear its cached reset state when it observes a new generation. The next write emits noise before its payload, then resumes the existing reset behavior.
- Serialize the complete masked write against hopping, keeping all noise packets, configured delays, and the associated payload on the same socket and destination.

Generation tracking also handles returning to a previously used endpoint. Failed hops retain the active path and generation; attempts that leave the endpoints unchanged do not trigger additional noise.

Both configured noise items and Lua scripts use the existing emission code. Mask ordering, socket deadline propagation, receive handling, and connection cleanup remain unchanged. The existing connection stays in place, preserving Hysteria continuity. No configuration fields are added.

**Regression coverage**

- Source-port-only, destination-port-only, destination-IP-only, and combined changes.
- Continuous traffic, repeated writes on one path, and returning to a previous endpoint.
- Unchanged endpoints and failed hops.
- Concurrent hopping during delayed noise emission.
- Configured items and Lua scripts, mask ordering, reset behavior, deadline propagation, and socket cleanup.

**Verification**

- Focused noise/udphop tests and race detection passed.
- Finalmask and Hysteria package checks passed in short mode.
- GitHub’s formatting/protobuf check passed after applying the repository formatter.
- The full package run timed out in the separate Sudoku end-to-end harness; that run did not complete.

issues.title: Sockopt: Report the real ioctl error from OriginalDst on Darwin
issues.body:
### Problem

`OriginalDst` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go` reports success when the `DIOCNATLOOK` ioctl fails:

```go
if _, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(syscall.SYS_IOCTL, fd, DIOCNATLOOK, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&nl))); errno != 0 {
	return net.IP{}, -1, os.NewSyscallError("ioctl", err)
}
```

`err` is the `os.Open("/dev/pf")` result from the top of the function, which already returned early if it was non-nil, so `err` is always `nil` here — and `os.NewSyscallError` returns `nil` for a nil error. The `errno` the ioctl returned is dropped.

Both callers (`tcp.GetOriginalDestination`, `udp.RetrieveOriginalDest`) only test `err != nil`, so they build a destination from the zero IP and port `-1`: `net.IPAddress(net.IP{})` returns a nil `Address`, `net.Port(-1)` wraps to 65535, and `IsValid()` does not catch it since it only checks `Network != Network_Unknown`.

### Fix

Report `errno`. It is already the branch condition, so the error is always non-nil.

### Notes

Two further issues in this function, left alone because Darwin's `struct pfioc_natlook` cannot be verified (no `net/pfvar.h` in the SDK) and the path has no test coverage: `nl.proto` is always `IPPROTO_TCP` although `hub_darwin.go` reaches this function for UDP, and `nl.af` is never set to `AF_INET6` although the result is switched on `nl.af`. `sockopt_freebsd.go` sets both.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go run ./infra/vformat -mode check` and `go test ./...` are clean on this branch; the three geodata-dependent packages fail identically on unmodified `main` here because `geoip.dat` / `geosite.dat` are absent locally.

issues.title: chore(finalmask): code clean
tun: end UDP flows and cancel dispatches when the inbound closes
issues.body:
## Problem

Closing a core instance that has a `tun` inbound leaves its UDP flows alive, and everything they hold with them.

- `Handler.Init` detaches the handler's context from the instance (`core.ToBackgroundDetachedContext`), and nothing cancels it on `Close`.
- `stack.Close` resets the TCP connections and closes the sockets opened by `DialUDP`, but never touches the UDP flow table (`udpConnectionHandler.udpConns`).

So each UDP flow's reader keeps waiting on its packet queue after `Close`, which pins its XUDP mux session, the mux `ClientWorker` and that worker's connection to the server.

Measured in a client that embeds the tun inbound and restarts the instance per session (goroutine origins from `runtime.Stack`): about 80 goroutines, 0.8 MB of live heap and stacks, and one established outbound connection leaked per instance, with no decay over 8+ minutes. After 25 instances: 1600 goroutines, all created by `tun.(*udpConnectionHandler).HandlePacket`, `mux.(*ClientWorker).Dispatch`, `mux.NewClientWorker` and `mux.(*DialingWorkerFactory).Create`, and 17 established connections to the server.

## Fix

- `Handler` owns a `cancel` for its detached context and calls it in `Close` before closing the stack, so in-flight dispatches unwind (also the ones not blocked on the reader).
- `stack.Close` ends every UDP flow (`udpConnectionHandler.closeAll`): their readers get EOF, the dispatches return and release their outbounds. The flow table also refuses new flows from then on, mirroring `handleTCP`'s `closed` check: a packet already in flight between the stack closing and the tun closing used to open a fresh flow (and, with a mux outbound, dial a worker) during shutdown.

The remaining XUDP mux workers then close on the mux client's idle check (two 16 s monitor ticks after their last session), after which goroutines and heap are back at the baseline and no server connections remain.

## Verification

- New tests: `TestUDPHandlerCloseAllEndsFlows` (flows end on close, a late packet opens none) and `TestHandlerCloseCancelsDispatches` (a dispatch that is not reading returns when the handler closes). `go test -race ./proxy/tun/` passes.
- With the patch, 20 instance start/stop cycles end with 0 established connections to the server and the baseline goroutine count; without it, 17 connections and 1600 goroutines that never go away.

issues.title: TUN inbound: Half-close the app connection when the outbound is done, instead of waiting for `uplinkOnly`
issues.body:
## Why

With Xray's TUN as the system VPN, an app that reads a response until the server closes waits about 1 s more than it should on every such connection. The outbound already knows the response is over, but TUN keeps the app's connection open until the whole dispatch ends, and that happens only after `uplinkOnly`. Examples are HTTP/1.0 without `Content-Length`, RTSP (Moonlight in #5845) and simple request and reply protocols. With this change the app gets the end of the response right away

## What changed

- TUN sends FIN to the app as soon as the outbound is done with the response. The app can still send, and the connection is closed as before when the dispatch is over
- the lightweight TCP stack gets `CloseWrite` for that
- the rest of the core still closes links in pairs, as agreed in the thread

## Testing and limits

- `TestTCPCloseWrite` checks that FIN goes out, that data from the app is still read after it and that `Close` sends nothing more. `go test -race ./proxy/tun` passes
- this helps only when the outbound itself sees the end of the response, for example freedom or VMess. Over VLESS the outbound ends only after `uplinkOnly` on the server, so the wait there stays

Related #5845 #7345

issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

AI disclosure: this PR was completed using Claude Opus 5.5.

issues.title: XHTTP server: unblock writes and serialize connection close
issues.body:
## Summary

An XHTTP response write can hold the connection mutex while blocked on a slow reader. Closing the logical connection then waits on that mutex, including when a proxy inactivity timeout cancels the business context while the HTTP request stays open.

Signal closure before waiting for the writer and interrupt an active write using `http.ResponseController`. Serialize the complete transition with `sync.Once` so concurrent business/handler closes join the deadline call and the writer before `ServeHTTP` returns.

```text
Close (once)
  signal closure
  interrupt active write
  wait for writer completion
```

## Evidence

- Added `TestConcurrentCloseWaitsForDeadline`, using a real HTTP test server and a gated response writer. The gates ensure the business close owns the first deadline call before the handler closes.
- Upstream implementation: fails with `Close waited for the blocked writer without interrupting it`.
- An unserialized close transition: fails with `deadline call outlived ServeHTTP during concurrent Close`.
- Commit `8628110`, rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 on Linux/amd64: `go test -buildvcs=false ./transport/internet/splithttp -count=1` passes (`ok`, 2.434s).
- Bounded loopback `packet-up` fixtures run against a binary rebuilt from commit `8628110`: peer half-close and an internal inactivity timeout with the HTTP request still open both finish with `CLOSE_FRAMES=0`, `WRITE_FRAMES=0`, and `CLOSE_WAIT_CONNECTIONS=0`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** Two-way.

**Blast Radius:** XHTTP shutdown. Active I/O is interrupted on close; the existing transport tests cover normal completion.

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: Replace outdated XTool with 3x-setup in the One Click section
issues.body: ## Summary Replace the outdated XTool entry (not updated for 3 years) with [3x-setup](https://github.com/Anthrop44/3x-setup), a secure-by-default, Nushell-based deployment and management solution for Xray-core. It automates a modern Xray-core best-practice architecture, combining direct VLESS + XHTTP + TLS with Cloudflare-proxied VLESS Encryption + XTLS Vision + XHTTP. ## Features - **Secure by default:** Enforces SSH key-only authentication, restrictive firewall rules with Cloudflare-only origin access, and localhost-only management interfaces accessible through SSH tunneling. - **Resilient deployment:** Remote initialization continues independently after SSH disconnects, with detailed per-stage logs and verification. - **Easy configuration and maintenance:** Schema-validated JSON configuration, one-command client/CDN configuration synchronization, and persistent subscription URLs across server rebuilds. - **Fully automated:** Handles Caddy camouflage, Xray inbounds, 3X-UI clients, TLS certificate issuance and renewal, and end-to-end connectivity checks. I've been developing this for months and will keep maintaining. Should be reliable enough. I'll never accept any sponsorship for it too.

issues.title: grpc: close cached clients with their outbound handler
issues.body:
Related to #7177. Requesting review of resource ownership, shutdown semantics, and API compatibility

## Problem

Outbound gRPC clients are cached by destination and MemoryStreamConfig, but core shutdown never closes or removes them. In an embedding process that stays alive, clients can retain connections and continue reconnecting after their core has stopped.

## Change

Give memory stream settings synchronous close-hook registration, and close the resources from their owning outbound handler. Register each ClientConn for exact-entry cache removal and ClientConn.Close. Refuse both reuse and creation after owner closure starts; racing creation must either register for cleanup or close its unpublished client. Cleanup runs outside the settings/cache locks, and concurrent Close callers wait for the same result.

The supported Instance lifecycle is single-start. Each fresh core retains separate ownership even when endpoint and outbound tags match. No per-run generation model, idle-timeout change or per-RPC closure of the shared ClientConn is added.

## Validation

- Synthetic regression reproduces the problem on v26.3.27 and main da2248c.
- `go test -race ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/grpc -count=1 -timeout=120s` passes on this exact branch.
- Official `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./` passes.
- Tests cover two live cores, sibling streams, normal/MultiMode, fresh-core cycles, failed-start cleanup, multiple destinations, owner/acquisition races, cancellation/backoff and forced dialerProxy lookup contention with Manager.Close.
- Earlier candidate testing also ran the target race suites five times and the dialerProxy test ten times. Those results are supplementary, not a claim that the whole upstream suite passes.

## Review questions / limits

- Handler.Close previously always returned nil. This candidate propagates cleanup errors. Is propagation preferred, or should transport cleanup be logged while preserving the existing return policy? Embedders must distinguish a cleanup error from a still-running core.
- MemoryStreamConfig with resource/mutex state must not be copied; direct external transport callers must close their settings.
- Manager.RemoveHandler still bypasses Handler.Close. XHTTP/nested download settings and TUN eventfd cleanup remain unfixed.
- No general multi-instance guarantee for Xray's other process-global networking state, TLS/Reality/masking matrix, or physical Android packet boundary is claimed.

This is intended as a draft for ownership/API review, not a claim that the Android product defect is resolved.

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.title: Outbound: Close the handler when removing it; VLESS Reverse Proxy: Don't start after closing
issues.body:
`outbound.Manager.RemoveHandler`, which `xray api rmo` (`HandlerService.RemoveOutbound`) calls, deletes the handler from the map but never closes it, while `inbound.Manager.RemoveHandler` does. So whatever the removed outbound's `Close()` would release keeps running:

- WireGuard creates its TUN in the constructor (a kernel TUN when available, otherwise a gVisor stack), and once used also has the device with its UDP socket and keepalives.
- VLESS with `reverse` keeps its monitor task: the removed outbound keeps dialing the server every 2 s.
- Same for MASQUE's tunnel. VLESS with `testpre` gets closed too, but its pre-connects only stop reliably with #7113: on main, `Close()` stops just the goroutines waiting to hand over a connection, not the ones redialing an unreachable server.

This shows up wherever outbounds are added and removed at runtime through the API, e.g. by panels.

### Changes

- `RemoveHandler` closes the handler it removed. It does so after releasing the manager lock, so a slow `Close()` (WireGuard) doesn't hold up `Select()`/`GetHandler()` for new connections. Removing an unknown tag still returns nil, and a removed handler is closed only once, since `Manager.Close()` no longer sees it.
- VLESS starts the reverse 2 s after the outbound is created (a goroutine in `New()`), so an outbound removed within those 2 s would still start it after `Close()`. `Reverse.Start()` is now a no-op once `Reverse.Close()` has run.

The other callers of `RemoveHandler` (commander, metrics, reverse portal, VLESS inbound's reverse) remove their own internal outbounds, whose `Close()` is a no-op or idempotent.

Connections already in flight on a removed outbound behave as before unless its `Close()` tears them down (WireGuard, MASQUE). A reverse bridge that is already connected is left to end on its own; only new ones stop.

### Reproduction (on 836a6fe)

Client: `api` with `HandlerService` behind a dokodemo-door inbound, `freedom` as the only configured outbound. Server: a plain TCP listener that only counts accepted connections.

**VLESS `reverse`**: the outbound is added with `xray api ado` and removed with `xray api rmo`. Afterwards `xray api lso` lists only the `freedom` outbound in all runs.

| `rmo` after `ado` | build | accepts at `rmo` | 3 s later | 13 s later |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 s | main | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| 7 s | this PR | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| 0.5 s | main | 0 | 1 | 6 |
| 0.5 s | this PR | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**WireGuard** (`noKernelTun: true`): five outbounds, each added with `ado` and removed right away with `rmo`. Goroutines from the `metrics` listener's `/debug/pprof/goroutine`: main 11 → 72, this PR 11 → 12.

### Tests

- New `TestRemoveHandlerClosesHandler` (on main the handler is closed 0 times) and `TestReverseNotStartedAfterClose` (on main the monitor runs once).
- `go test ./...` except `testing/scenarios`: the only failures also fail on main, tests that need `resources/geo*.dat` or network access.
- `go test ./testing/scenarios`: pass.
- `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./`: pass.

issues.title: Fix: resolve bugs, data races and leaks found by a codebase audit
issues.body:
## Summary

A systematic audit of `proxy/`, `app/`, `transport/` and `common/` (connection lifecycles, UDP relays, protocol frame parsing, hot paths) uncovered ~40 verifiable issues. This PR fixes them in small, contained patches.

## Security

- **shadowsocks_2022 UDP (OOM DoS)**: NAT sessions were created *before* authentication and without any cap (`GetOrCreate` on the raw AES-ECB header). ~10k random pkt/s \u2192 ~5M live sessions in the 500s window \u2192 multi-GB heap. Sessions are now created only after the AEAD/EIH check succeeds (`packet.go`, `inbound_multi.go`; `RelayInbound` already validated EIH first and is unchanged).
- **UDP truncation**: `shadowsocks.EncodeUDPPacket` silently truncated datagrams whose header+payload exceeded 8 KB (unchecked `ErrBufferFull`), and hysteria's UDP writer silently dropped messages that did not fit. Both now return an explicit error; trojan's `writePacket` pre-checks the size with a clear error.
- **XtlsFilterTls**: the attacker-controlled session-id length could make the cipher-suite read go past the buffer end (stale pool bytes), flipping `EnableXtls` detection. Bounds-checked now.
- **protocol/address.go**: a zero-length domain (attacker-controlled byte) made `BytesFrom(-0)` return the whole scratch buffer and panic on `domain[0]` \u2014 and the inbound path has no `recover()`. Now rejected with an error.
- **observatory**: `GetObservation` handed the shared, concurrently mutated `[]*OutboundStatus` to all balancers; it now returns a snapshot under `statusLock`.
- **grpc dial**: a failed `grpc.NewClient` stored a nil conn in `globalDialerMap`; the next lookup would panic. Error is now returned before caching.

## Data races (verified with `go test -race`)

- `session.CanSpliceCopy`: written by the downlink task and read by the uplink task (and vice versa); now accessed via `atomic.StoreInt32/LoadInt32` everywhere (47 sites, field documented as atomic-only).
- `tls.Config`: OCSP/hot-reload tickers replaced certificates in the slice while concurrent handshakes read them, and `isCertificateExpired` mutated the shared `Leaf`. Certificates now live in a small `certificateBundle` guarded by an RWMutex; the OCSP callback swaps in a *copy* of the certificate instead of mutating it; `isCertificateExpired` no longer writes.
- `common/cache/lru`: `PeekKeyFromValue` read list elements without the lock (race-detector-confirmed, fakedns hot path); `Put` also left a stale `valueToElement` entry when updating an existing key.
- mux: `x.Status = Active` written without `XUDPManager` lock; hard type assertions in `Session.Close` replaced with a checked one.
- reverse bridge/portal: worker state fields accessed from monitor/heartbeat/picker goroutines; now atomic.
- kcp: `rd`/`wd` deadlines written by `SetDeadline` and read by wait loops; now `atomic.Int64` nanoseconds.
- websocket: `delayDialConn.closed` is atomic now.
- dns outbound: `c.conn` read outside the lock; captured under the lock.
- router webhook: `wg.Add(1)` could race with `Close`\u2019s `wg.Wait()`; Add and the closed check are serialized by a mutex.
- tests (splithttp, blackhole): unsynchronized test state flagged by `-race` fixed.

## Leaks

- splithttp: quic.Transport + UDP socket leaked on every failed H3 dial (fix mirrors masque/xdrive); pooled HTTP/1.1 upload conns were never closed (tracked and closed on `Close()` and on write/read failure).
- mux: the picker's periodic cleanup returned an error when idle, which permanently killed the 30s cleanup task.
- proxyman inbound: `udpWorker.Close()` never closed active UDP sessions (goroutine + pipe per session leaked on every Instance restart).
- dns: with `serveStale` and no `serveExpiredTTL` the cache cleanup never ran \u2014 unbounded growth; cleanup now always runs and evicts entries stale for more than 24h.
- wireguard: device leaked if `IpcSet`/`Up` failed in `Start()`.
- vless: `GetReverse` waited forever for outbound handlers (now bounded, 10s); `testpre` goroutines hot-looped

issues.title: XHTTP: bound TLS handshakes on TCP connections
issues.body:
The ChatGPT desktop app stopped loading workspace settings after an upgrade from one Wayrill version to the next. Restarting Wayrill routing, which restarted Xray, restored access. The traffic log showed the expected policy group, which includes XHTTP over TLS/HTTP/2 outbounds. The app reconnected normally as soon as the next upgrade, to Wayrill 0.37.17 with this patch, finished. The original capture begins after startup, so the evidence for the TLS stall comes from the controlled reproduction below.

## Reproduction and relation to #6590

The loopback reproduction uses an Xray VLESS/XHTTP client and server with the default three XMUX clients. A TCP relay accepts the first three connections, reads each TLS ClientHello and leaves those sockets open without sending a ServerHello. The relay forwards every new connection to the healthy Xray server. HTTP/2 requests sharing a pending dial keep waiting on the old sockets, even after the original application requests time out. Fresh requests then fail despite a working server being available to fresh dials.

This is the same stalled handshake reported in #6590. The additional finding is that the failure can persist across application retries after the peer is healthy for new connections. A TCP stack can keep acknowledging probes while the application or an intermediary makes no progress on a particular TLS handshake. The reproduction uses default TCP keepalive settings and injects a transient fault in the relay. [Closing discussion](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/6590#issuecomment-5178980812)

## Fix

Start a ten-second child context once the TCP connection is established, using the same handshake budget as Go's default HTTP transport. Complete standard TLS explicitly and use the same context for uTLS and REALITY. On expiry the stalled handshake ends and releases the socket, so HTTP/2 can retire the shared pending dial and subsequent requests can dial again. The context ends at handshake completion. Established streams continue under the existing HTTP request lifetime, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC's own handshake timeout.

## Validation

- On upstream `main` at `5d17b872`, six fresh requests timed out over 10.5 seconds. The relay saw no new dials. Restarting the client core restored traffic.
- With the patch, all three stalled sockets closed and a fresh request returned HTTP 200 in the same process. Verified this with Go TLS, uTLS and REALITY over HTTP/2. Also verified that the stalled sockets closed over HTTP/1.1.
- Verified healthy streams transferred data after 12 seconds in each of those configurations. The XHTTP Go suite passed alongside a local regression covering all three TLS paths against silent peers.

issues.title: Feature Request: Add udp+local:// DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)
issues.body:
# Feature Request: Add `udp+local://` DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)

## Summary

Xray's DNS configuration supports `+local` variants for HTTPS, h2c, QUIC and TCP, but there is **no `udp+local` scheme** for plain UDP DNS in local mode. This means there is currently **no way to send plain UDP DNS queries to a local resolver while bypassing the routing/dispatcher stack**.

## Current state

`app/dns/nameserver.go`, `NewServer()` switch (main branch):

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https"):      // DoH remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c"):        // DoH h2c remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https+local"): // DoH local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c+local"):   // DoH h2c local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "quic+local"):  // DoQ local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp"):         // TCP remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp+local"):   // TCP local
case strings.EqualFold(u.String(), "fakedns"):
```

Every protocol except plain UDP has a `+local` form. Plain UDP falls through to the default branch:

```go
if dest.Network == net.Network_UDP {
    return NewClassicNameServer(dest, dispatcher, ...)
}
```

Note that `NewClassicNameServer` receives the `dispatcher`, so plain UDP **always goes through the routing stack** — there is no way to bypass it.

## Why this matters (measured data)

For a local resolver (e.g. smartdns on `127.0.0.1`), bypassing the dispatcher matters. Measured on a local resolver over loopback, one A + one AAAA query for the same domain:

| Path | p50 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tcp+local://` (current workaround) | ~810µs | 2 TCP handshakes + 2 closes |
| `tcp+local://` pipelined on 1 conn | ~680µs | would need connection pooling, not implemented |
| **plain UDP, 2 packets sent in parallel** | **~376µs** | no handshake, no teardown |

The UDP path is ~2x faster than the current `tcp+local` workaround because it avoids TCP handshake/teardown entirely. Pairing responses by DNS ID worked in 200/200 trials with zero mismatch.

For users running a local caching resolver, this overhead is paid on every cache-miss lookup.

## Secondary issue: port parsing for bare `udp://` schemes

Related bug found while investigating. With:

```json
"dns": { "servers": ["udp://127.0.0.1:5353"] }
```

xray logs:

```
DNS: created UDP client initialized for udp://127.0.0.1:5353:53
```

The port becomes `5353:53` — the `:5353` is swallowed into the address (as a domain string) and then a default `:53` is appended by:

```go
// app/dns/nameserver_udp.go:41
if address.Port == 0 {
    address.Port = net.Port(53)
}
```

This is because `infra/conf/dns.go` builds the endpoint with `Address` and `Port` as separate fields, and `Address.Build()` calls `net.ParseAddress()` on the whole string including `:5353`, while `Port` stays 0.

Attempting `udp://127.0.0.1` (no port) resolves to `udp://127.0.0.1:53`, which happens to work, but the scheme is still parsed as a domain so the connection fails with:

```
failed to open connection to udp:udp://127.0.0.1:53
> too many colons in address
```

Contrast with `tcp+local`, which parses correctly because it uses `url.Hostname()` and `url.Port()` separately (`app/dns/nameserver_tcp.go:75-81`).

## Proposed change

Add a `udp+local` case that mirrors `tcp+local` — parse host/port via `url.Hostname()` / `url.Port()` and pass `nil` as the dispatcher:

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "udp+local"): // DNS-over-UDP Local mode
    return NewUDPNameServer(u, nil, disableCache, serveStale, serveExpiredTTL, clientIP), nil
```

Where the new constructor resolves the destination the same way `baseTCPNameServer` does:

```go
port := net.Port(53)
if url.Port() != "" {
    if port, err = net.PortFromString(url.Port()); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
dest := net.UDPDestination(net.ParseAddress(url.Hostname()), port)
```

This would also give users a documented way to hit a local resolver on a non-53 port without the address-swallowing bug.

## Environment

comments.issue_title: panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
comments.body:
The path is `buf.NewExisted`: it only enforces a *minimum* capacity, so it returns buffers longer than `buf.Size` — and the gRPC transport wraps hunks of arbitrary size with it (`grpc/encoding/hunkconn.go:97`, `multiconn.go:78`). You have a gRPC inbound.

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` splits such a buffer once and writes the whole remainder into one new buffer, discarding the `ErrBufferFull` from `Write`:

```go
buffer2 := buf.New()
buffer2.Write(buffer1.BytesFrom(index))
```

With no TLS record header in range, `index` is `buf.Size/2` = 4096, so a 12288-byte buffer leaves a remainder of exactly 8192: `buffer2.Len() == buf.Size`, and above that size the surplus is dropped with the error. `XtlsPadding` then gets `paddingLen = 8192 - 21 - 8192 = -21`, and `Extend(-21)` slices `b.v[8192:8171]`.

Reproduced on current main (`f781c687`): 8213 bytes is fine, 12288 panics with your exact string. So the threshold is 12288 = 4096 + 8192, which fits a clustered few-per-hour rate rather than every connection.

On the hardening you suggested: clamping `paddingLen` at 0 stops the crash but keeps the truncation — 7712 of 20000 bytes dropped — trading a crash for stream corruption. The fix belongs in `ReshapeMultiBuffer`, which should keep splitting until the remainder fits.

// If s.config.Address is set to a domain (e.g. "localhost" or "example.com"),
// AsAddress() returns a domainAddress, and calling .IP() on it panics.
udpHub, err := internet.ListenSystemPacket(
    context.Background(),
    &net.UDPAddr{IP: responseAddress.IP(), Port: 0},  // 💥 panic here
    nil,
)
```

This is because `domainAddress.IP()` in `common/net/address.go` unconditionally panics:

```go
func (domainAddress) IP() net.IP {
    panic("Calling IP() on a DomainAddress.")
}
```

**Why it is NOT an authentication bypass:**

The panic occurs at line 206, which is reached only *after* `auth5()` completes successfully at line 148. An unauthenticated or wrongly-authenticated client is rejected before the panic site is ever reached (confirmed by testing all three scenarios: no-auth client, wrong-password client, and no-auth server).

**Trigger conditions:**

The vulnerable path requires the server operator to have explicitly set `address` to a domain name (e.g. `"localhost"`) in the SOCKS inbound config. A remote attacker has no control over `responseAddress` — it comes from `s.config.Address` (server config), not from client input. The client only needs to send a `UDP ASSOCIATE` command to trigger the crash once the misconfiguration is in place.

**Impact:** This is a **misconfiguration-induced crash** (DoS), not a security vulnerability. If `address` is left empty (default) or set to a valid IP, the panic never occurs.

comments.issue_title: VLESS: run multiplexing directly on transport
comments.body:
@RPRX, I ran additional security and functionality checks with AI assistance. **The checks performed did not reveal any new issues attributable to our DispatchLink migration or the Multiplex/Reverse changes.** They did identify several defects already present in the original implementation.

<details>
<summary>Checks and findings</summary>

The checks covered an Original client connecting to our server and our client connecting to our server: 16 VMess profiles, including AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305, ordinary UDP/SingleXUDP, and default/AuthenticatedLength modes. Additional encrypted XDrive, configuration compatibility, request cancellation, and preconnection lifecycle checks passed. Header, body-integrity, and immediate replay checks did not demonstrate an authentication bypass.

The inherited findings are:

1. **VLESS/Reverse: a `testpre` initialization race.** The constructor starts background Reverse work before assigning the field that the callback reads. The race detector reported the conflicting accesses. Original has the same initialization order. The minimal proposed fix is to move the existing assignment before launching the goroutine; no additional synchronization machinery is needed.

2. **Shared UDP dispatcher: a `connEntry.closed` race.** This was reproduced on both our version and Original. A separately tested composition with #7411 passed the corresponding checks; that fix has not been added to this PR.

3. **VMess: nonce reuse after the 16-bit record counter wraps.** Actual AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 codec checks confirmed reuse on the 65,537th record. The relevant nonce generation and body setup are unchanged from Original. A repair requires an explicit decision about long-lived connections and peer compatibility.

4. **Experimental AuthenticatedLength: cross-direction key/nonce reuse for encrypted lengths.** The first encrypted length fields matched across request and response for both ciphers, consistent with the identical request-derived key/IV and initial counter. Payload-body keys remain direction-separated. This mechanism is also inherited, and the experiment is disabled by default. Fixing it requires a separate decision about disabling/rejecting the experiment or introducing compatible directional derivation.

The cryptographic checks demonstrated violations of nonce uniqueness, not a traffic-forgery exploit or authentication bypass. For the initialization race and cryptographic findings, attribution to Original is based on source comparison; the shared UDP race was also reproduced at runtime on Original.

</details>

I suggest addressing these findings in separate PRs, since the defects were already present in the original implementation and were not introduced by our DispatchLink migration.

These checks were carried out with AI assistance. My knowledge of cryptography is not sufficient to independently validate the VMess cryptographic conclusions or the correctness and peer compatibility of changes to its encryption. I can try to prepare separate fixes and tests with AI assistance, but the cryptographic changes will need independent review by someone familiar with the cryptography and protocol. Passing tests and AI review alone are not enough for that.

>Delay only paces the local schedule: after `ea2c7edc` nothing reads padding, so it cannot affect any decision — it only spreads the encrypted bursts in time (sizes are unchanged). Without it the whole startup burst goes out in a few ms.

>Where it sits: for every turn except the last, "pause after turn i" and "pause before turn i+1" are the same wire gap — the preset uses the latter (`startDelay`), the config uses the former. The difference is only at the boundaries: turn 0 goes out right after Login Acknowledged (like a real client), and the last turn used to get a trailing pause. That one was wrong: nothing follows it, so it only delayed the first proxied packet — `delay: "300"` on the final turn moved the first packet from 3 ms to 304 ms (measured through a relay). Fixed locally by pausing only between turns.

>Which value the wait uses: the side that sends a turn samples `[delay_min, delay_max]`; the peer, which sends nothing for that turn, waits exactly `delay_min` — the proto comment said "at least", the code is "exactly". Consequence measured with `20-200`: the gap you see after the turn is 20 (the min), and the sampled excess lands on the sender's own next turn (20 then 138). So a fixed value reproduces a captured gap; a range only jitters the sending side.

>On the struck-through part: agreed. The pause is local, so the observed cross-direction gap is local pause + one one-way delay — RTT is the wrong unit, and compensating for it is not stable either.

comments.issue_title: VLESS: run multiplexing directly on transport
comments.body:
@RPRX, most of these changes come from switching to `DispatchLink` and removing pipes and copy tasks. Some responsibilities of the old pipeline now have to be handled explicitly in the direct path. Below is what was retained and why.

<details>
<summary>Why the remaining code is needed</summary>

1. **The migration following #5143 is already implemented.**  
   Ordinary VMess passes its codecs directly to `DispatchLink`. The intermediate pipes, two copy tasks, and post-authentication inactivity timer have been removed.

2. **Serialization is needed before encryption.**  
   The DNS outbound can write several responses concurrently through the same codec. A test with four simultaneous DNS queries, without this lock, exposed codec-state races and authentication failures. Locking only the physical write does not prevent them.

3. **Response completion and cancellation remain separate responsibilities.**  
   The response header must be sent even for an empty response, the conditional termination marker must be preserved, and flush errors must be checked. Returning from `DispatchLink` does not always mean that the response has finished. In a separate guard-removal test, 144 bytes of decoded input reached a real TCP sink after cancellation; the current guard blocked them.

4. **The small change in `default.go` preserves accounting and read interruption.**  
   The dispatcher assigns the USER counter to the native flow, which accounts for incoming data before the outbound consumes it. Simply reverting this part produced **0 instead of 4096** unread bytes. Removing it would require moving counter assignment and the corresponding plumbing into Multiplex, which is shared by VLESS and VMess.

5. **The split between shared and native responsibilities was already evaluated.**  
   Physical-write serialization was moved into the native `PhysicalWriter`, used by VLESS and VMess. The narrow dispatcher integration and shared outbound cleanup were retained: the outbound handler knows the actual operation outcome. Moving that cleanup into Multiplex would require additional plumbing.

</details>

Pushed a whole-mechanism simplification of the DATA and cancellation paths.

Commit: https://github.com/svlavr/Xray-core/commit/dd9d0216638f412c1f9bedccc6afbe4217a81d0d

Client DATA now goes directly through the shared Session writer, removing the encoded DATA queue and its mutex/condition/refill machinery. Server TCP uses that same writer instead of a separate output facade. VMess cancellation no longer synchronously waits for foreign cleanup in the reproduced writer-abort case.

UDP response storage remains deliberately: removing it delivered only 9/65 packets in the held-output experiment. Restoring the existing packet store delivered 65/65 while preserving the client/TCP simplification.

Source accounting against the pinned original comparison (`f082058`):

- This final pass removes 107 runtime lines compared with the preceding local implementation.
- The complete PR still touches 60 files: +3191/-3475, net -284.
- Manual runtime code is 7023 lines versus the original 6997: net +26, previously +133. This is not a claim that the PR was halved or that all 60 entries are strictly required by DispatchLink.

Six matched Windows-host trials, each transferring 1 GiB over eight bulk flows plus a loaded probe, show paired-median throughput +6.3% and loaded p95 latency -15%. Combined CPU/GiB is +1.6% with mixed pair directions, so no CPU saving is established.

The separate 40-target/8-GiB diagnostic comparison shows server allocation 87.51895 -> 86.39965 MiB per verified GiB (about -1.3%), with held goroutines unchanged at 134. This does not establish lower overall server RAM: paired-median server private-memory peak is about 1.5 MiB higher, and held private memory in the diagnostic pair is about 2.2 MiB higher. The reported larger production-memory increase remains unattributed. These are controlled host results, not WAN/device guarantees.

Validation includes nine original tests under `-race` on the integrated source, 65 positive race-enabled consumer test events, and nine selected peer/scenario groups covering VLESS, UDP/XUDP, VMess and Reverse; one group is a compiled-source component rather than an executable peer. [Windows] Kill Switch blocks AmneziaWG handshake — endless "Connecting", tunnel never comes up, DNS/Internet blocked on all adapters
issues.body:
### Summary

With **Kill Switch enabled**, connecting to an AmneziaWG server on Windows never completes: the client stays in "Connecting" (spinner) forever, and at the same time DNS and all Internet access die on **every** adapter — Windows reports "No Internet" while the cable is connected and DHCP keeps working.

Disabling Kill Switch makes the **same server** connect in ~1–2 seconds and everything works. Re-enabling Kill Switch and pressing Connect reproduces the failure every time.

This looks like a bootstrap deadlock:

- the Kill Switch WFP rules permit traffic only through the VPN interface (and appear to whitelist `AmneziaVPN.exe`);
- the WireGuard/AmneziaWG handshake is performed by the client **service** `AmneziaVPN-service.exe` (`tunneldaemon`, service `AmneziaWGTunnel$AmneziaVPN`) over the **physical** adapter to the server endpoint;
- those handshake packets are blocked, so the tunnel never comes up;
- meanwhile the blocking rules are already active, so DNS/Internet is dead on all adapters.

The state is only cleared by Disconnect (or, in an earlier failure, by a reboot) — consistent with stale WFP filters (cf. #3198).

### Environment

- AmneziaVPN **5.1.0.6** (Windows x64; the app says this is the latest version, and indeed 5.1.1.9 has no Windows build)
- Windows 11, build **26300.9974**, DisplayVersion 26H2 (registry ProductName says "Windows 10 Pro")
- Protocol: **AmneziaWG** (self-hosted server, EU), `Table = off`, `Address = 10.8.1.x`, `DNS = 1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1`, `MTU = 1376`
- No third-party firewall / antivirus / VPN / system proxy running; Windows Firewall defaults

### To Reproduce

1. Add an AmneziaWG server (works fine with Kill Switch off).
2. Settings → enable **Kill Switch**.
3. Press **Connect**.
4. Client stays in "Connecting" indefinitely. `ping 8.8.8.8`, browsers and DNS stop working on both Ethernet and Wi-Fi; Windows shows "No Internet".
5. Press **Disconnect** → DNS and Internet return immediately.
6. Disable Kill Switch → **Connect** → tunnel comes up in 1–2 s, egress IP is the server IP, everything works.
7. Re-enable Kill Switch → **Connect** → same failure again.

### Evidence (Windows Event Log, 2026-11-17, local time UTC+7)

| Time | Source | Event |
|---|---|---|
| 17:19:12.710 | NCSI 4042 | `{05b44401-…}` (AmneziaWG tunnel adapter): capability "Local", `ChangeReason: SuspectDnsProbeFailed` |
| 17:19:12.741 | NCSI 4042 | `{54d68279-…}` (Ethernet): capability "Local", `SuspectDnsProbeFailed` |
| 17:19:13.223 | NetworkProfile 4004 | "new connection profile has Internet: **false**" |
| 17:52:40 | SCM 7045 | Service **`Amnezia VPN (tunnel)`** installed: `"C:/Program Files/AmneziaVPN/AmneziaVPN-service.exe" tunneldaemon "[Interface] … DNS = 1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1 … Table = off"` |
| 17:52:41 | NetworkProfile 4001 | new network `{05b44401-…}` (tunnel adapter appears) |
| 17:52:42 | NetworkProfile 10001 | "network disconnected" — the tunnel adapter goes down ~1 s after creation |
| 17:55:35 | NCSI 4042 | Ethernet again: `SuspectDnsProbeFailed` (a few minutes after the failed Connect) |
| 17:59:44 | NCSI 4042 | Ethernet: `ActiveHttpProbeSucceeded` — Internet is back immediately after **Disconnect** |
| 17:59:52 | SCM 7045 | The same service is recreated on the next Connect; adapter comes up and down again |
| 18:27:29 | SCM 7045 | With **Kill Switch OFF**: service `AmneziaWGTunnel$AmneziaVPN` starts |
| 18:27:34 | NCSI 4042 | `{05b44401-…}`: capability "Internet", `ActiveHttpProbeSucceeded` |

With Kill Switch off the data plane is correct: default route `0.0.0.0/0 → 10.8.1.1` (metric 5), endpoint `<server-ip>/32` correctly goes via the physical gateway, egress IP is the server IP.

Note: the `[Interface]` section is passed in the service command line, including `PrivateKey` (see #3259 — this is readable by a non-admin user via `sc qc` on this machine as well). Key material is deliberately omitted here.

issues.title: fix(import): preserve single DNS server in WireGuard configs
issues.body:
## Problem
A native WireGuard/AmneziaWG `.conf` containing `DNS = 10.23.0.53` loses that resolver during import. The connection then receives the application's DNS instead. Retaining only `dns1` is insufficient: the existing native-profile fallback also adds the application's secondary resolver when `dns2` is absent.

Fixes #3345.

## Root cause
`extractWireGuardConfig()` searches the entire file with a regular expression requiring two IPv4 addresses and literal spacing around `=`. It can also pick up DNS-like text in comments or another key.

`NativeServerConfig::getDnsPair()` independently fills both missing fields from application settings.

## Changes
- Read the exact `DNS` entry from the existing line-parsed `configMap`.
- Split comma-separated values, trim whitespace, exclude trailing `#` comments, and retain the first two valid IPv4 addresses in their original order using the existing Qt-based `NetworkUtilities::checkIPv4Format()`.
- Preserve an empty secondary DNS for native WG/AWG profiles with a valid explicitly configured primary DNS. Do not duplicate the primary address.
- Keep the existing fallback for profiles with no valid primary DNS, other native protocols, and nonempty invalid stored secondary DNS values.
- Register one data-driven Qt Test suite in the existing CMake infrastructure.

No key, route, MTU, Endpoint, protocol-detection, configuration-format, or UI changes.

## Regression tests
The tests use the public production `ImportController::extractConfigFromData()`, real repositories/settings, profile JSON, `NativeServerConfig::fromJson()`, serialization round-trips, and `getDnsPair()`.

- 32 import rows: WG and AWG, single/pair DNS, spacing, ordering, absent/empty/invalid/mixed values, comments, another key, extra resolvers, and unsupported IPv6 values.
- 20 native fallback rows: WireGuard/AWG/AWG2 single/pair/missing/invalid DNS, plus unchanged OpenVPN/Xray behavior.
- One compatibility test for self-hosted admin/user and API profile fallbacks.
- Assert DNS fields and preservation of native config, keys, address, port, routes, MTU, keepalive, and WG/AWG detection.
- Synthetic keys and illustrative addresses only; no server, VPN connection, environment secrets, SSH, or Docker required.

## Validation
- **PASSED:** Release and Debug component builds on macOS arm64, Qt 6.12.0 / AppleClang 21. The external Qt/CMake harness compiles the complete production importer, native model, real repositories/settings, config models, serializers, IP validator, and pinned qtkeychain dependency. No extracted parser or mocked production model is used.
- **PASSED:** new Qt suite, 55 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped in Release and independently Debug (53 scenarios plus initialization/cleanup).
- **PASSED red → green:** the same tests with unmodified `upstream/dev` importer and native model at `7f9b7db482b8b1662b7466937e578008cbcb716e` produce 25 expected failures, including the single-DNS import and secondary fallback cases; the patched sources pass.
- **PASSED:** additional external probes using the real desktop `InterfaceConfig::toWgConf()` and Apple `WGConfig` plus the pinned WireGuardKit WgQuick parser, for one and two resolvers.
- **PASSED:** `git diff --check`, repository clang-format for the new test and changed production statements, changed-file/branch-isolation checks.
- **NOT RUN:** full application build, standard `test_common` and existing integration import suites (`MultipleImportsTest`, `ConfigFormatVersionTest`), and full CTest. Root configuration stops at missing Conan (`Could not find CONAN_COMMAND`).

## Compatibility
With application DNS `1.1.1.1` / `1.0.0.1`, an imported single `10.23.0.53` now yields `("10.23.0.53", "")`; two imported resolvers retain their order. Without valid imported DNS the application pair is still used.

issues.title: fix(security): prevent proxy secrets from leaking into logs
issues.body:
## Problem
Installing or reconfiguring a self-hosted MTProxy or Telemt service can put proxy access credentials in the application's diagnostic log when logging is enabled. Exporting the log archive can then disclose those credentials to its recipient.

Confirmed against `dev` at `7f9b7db482b8b1662b7466937e578008cbcb716e`.

## Root cause
The configure scripts intentionally return machine-readable credentials. MTProxy returns the base secret and credential-bearing Telegram links; the current Telemt script returns the base secret and empty link markers. `configureContainerWorker()` collects both stdout and stderr, then `updateContainerConfigAfterInstallation()` logs the entire buffer in the MTProxy and Telemt branches.

Qt debug messages are forwarded to `Logger`, which writes them without automatic redaction. `Logger::sensitive()` is opt-in and is not used here. `LogsController::zipAll()` includes the application log. A related Docker missing/stopped error message also dumped the same buffer.

## Security impact
A person with access to the local log, its console output while Logger is active, or a shared diagnostic archive can obtain proxy access credentials. This does not demonstrate unauthenticated remote log access or disclosure of SSH credentials. Application file logging is opt-in (disabled by default).

## Changes
- Remove the MTProxy and Telemt raw configure-output debug statements.
- Keep the Docker missing/stopped diagnostic, without the accumulated output.
- Leave all parsing, conditional field updates, configuration formats, transport modes, secret generation, and APIs unchanged.
- Add one test-class friendship to exercise the existing private static method without extracting or duplicating production parsing.

## Regression tests
Register `ProxyConfigurationLoggingTest` in the existing Qt/CMake test suite.

Twenty data-driven scenarios cover both services: padded/fake-TLS links, secret-only output matching the current Telemt script, links-only output, empty/incomplete/invalid/unmarked/noisy output, and repeated configuration with a different secret. Tests compare the full serialized configuration and assert that synthetic credentials, credential-bearing URLs, and a raw-output canary reach neither the Qt message handler nor the real Logger file. A control message ensures logging is active.

Only synthetic secrets and the reserved `proxy.example` host are used. Logger runs under Qt test mode with a unique application name; its test log is removed afterward.

## Validation
- **PASSED:** isolated Qt/CMake component builds on macOS arm64 with Qt 6.12.0 and AppleClang 21, in Release and Debug. These compile the complete, real `installController.cpp` translation unit, real config models, and Logger; unused controller dependencies are discarded by the linker. No extracted parser or mocked config model is used.
- **PASSED:** new regression suite in Release and Debug: 20 scenarios plus initialization/cleanup, 22 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped per configuration.
- **PASSED:** existing `LogsControllerTest` in the isolated Release harness, including ZIP round-trip with Qt private headers: 11 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped.
- **PASSED red → green:** compiling the same tests against the unmodified upstream controller in Release produces 14 expected failures on credentials/raw output in the actual log file; the patched controller passes. Release uses `-DNDEBUG -DQT_NO_DEBUG`, demonstrating that those flags do not suppress this logging.
- **PASSED:** `git diff --check`; repository clang-format for the new test and touched production lines; changed-file scope review.
- **NOT RUN:** complete application build/full upstream CTest suite. Root CMake configure fails because Conan is not installed (`Could not find CONAN_COMMAND`).

## Limitations
No live SSH/Docker installation, GUI export, cross-platform runtime test, or released application binary was exercised. The Docker error-output removal was compiled and reviewed but was not exercised th

issues.title: [Linux] AmneziaWG connection fails instantly: "hex string does not fit the slice" + daemon core dump (Mint 22.3, 5.1.0.6 & 5.0.3.0)
issues.body:
## Description
Connecting via AmneziaWG (container `amnezia-awg2`) fails instantly: the UI shows 
"Connecting" for ~1 second, then drops back to "Disconnected". 
The daemon log shows a peer public key parsing error, after which the daemon 
crashes with a core dump and is restarted by systemd.

The same server/config works fine on other family members' devices (non-Linux), 
so the server side is OK.

## Environment
- OS: Linux Mint 22.3 (x86_64)
- Client versions tested: 5.1.0.6 (ac175c8) and 5.0.3.0 (de93650) — same bug on both
- Protocol: AmneziaWG (container `amnezia-awg2`)
- Connection route mode: VpnOnlyForwardSites (site split tunneling also tested disabled — same result)
- Daemon binary: /opt/AmneziaVPN/bin/AmneziaVPN-service (systemd unit AmneziaVPN.service)

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open AmneziaVPN
2. Select server with AmneziaWG protocol
3. Click Connect
4. Connection drops after ~1 second

## What was already tried (no effect)
- Reinstalled the client (5.1.0.6 → 5.0.3.0)
- Removed server profile and re-added it with a freshly issued config
- Disabled site split tunneling completely
- Wiped user config (~/.config/AmneziaVPN.ORG)
- Restarted AmneziaVPN.service, rebooted the PC multiple times

## Actual result
Interface `amn0` is created, `amneziawg-go` starts, but peer configuration fails:
AmneziaVPN WireguardUtilsLinux : Created wireguard interface amn0
AmneziaVPN LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for /999999
AmneziaVPN LinuxRouteMonitor : Invalid destination prefix
AmneziaVPN WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) IPC error -22: failed to get peer by public key:
hex string does not fit the slice
AmneziaVPN WireguardUtilsLinux : Peer configuration failed: Unknown error -22
AmneziaVPN Daemon : Peer creation failed.
AmneziaVPN DaemonLocalServerConnection : Failed to activate the interface
malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted
AmneziaVPN.service: Main process exited, code=dumped, status=6/ABRT
AmneziaVPN.service: Failed with result 'core-dump'.
Note also the garbled peer key in the daemon log 
(`Configuring peer Ϯ⇈C5 via <server IP>`) — looks like memory corruption 
while parsing the peer public key, which then leads to the malloc() crash.

## Expected result
AmneziaWG tunnel connects normally, as it does on other devices with the same server.

## Additional info
The issue is specific to AmneziaWG — the daemon crashes during peer setup, 
before any handshake, so this is not a network/provider block.
